attendance.title: HR 3 — Attendance & Shifts
attendance.desc: Attendance in ZhiftERP: the four record types and the per-location method decision; Holiday List construction with the annual build procedure; Attendance records and the Employee Checkin log with its device, mobile, and manual sources; the Shift Type's auto-attendance block — determination, working-hours thresholds, grace periods, checkin windows, Process Attendance After, Last Sync of Checkin — with the test cycle; Default Shift and Shift Assignment with the coverage, orphan, and alignment reads; manual marking with the Employee Attendance Tool and the unmarked-day controls; and the Attendance Request lane with the daily, weekly, and monthly reads including the Monthly Attendance Sheet.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Attendance: scope and record structure
lessons.html:
This module covers attendance in ZhiftERP. On completing this module you will be able to: build Holiday Lists; create and read Attendance records; operate the Employee Checkin log; configure Shift Types with auto attendance; assign shifts; mark attendance manually with the Employee Attendance Tool; process Attendance Requests; and run the standing attendance reads including the Monthly Attendance Sheet.

The record structure. Attendance uses four record types. Learn their relationship before configuring anything:

1. Holiday List — the calendar of non-working days per working pattern (Chapter 2). Assigned per employee (module 1, Chapter 4). Days on the list are not attendance days.
2. Employee Checkin — one row per clock event: an IN or OUT with a timestamp, from a device or manual entry (Chapter 3). Checkins are raw logs; they are not attendance.
3. Attendance — one record per employee per working day, with a status: Present, Absent, On Leave, Half Day, or Work From Home (Chapter 3). Attendance records are the processed result, created by auto attendance (Chapter 4), by manual marking (Chapter 6), or by leave approval (module 4).
4. Shift Type and Shift Assignment — the working-hours definition and its assignment to employees (Chapters 4-5). The Shift Type carries the auto-attendance settings that convert checkins into Attendance records.

What reads attendance.

1. Payroll — where Payroll Settings sets the payroll basis to attendance, payment days derive from these records; where the basis is leave, absence still enters as leave records and the two modules meet at the records-close date (the Payroll track, module 3, Station 1, line 4).
2. The Monthly Attendance Sheet report — the month's grid per employee per day (Chapter 7).
3. Overtime evidence — where the overtime policy reads hours from checkins (the Payroll track, module 5, Chapter 3).
4. The disciplinary and pattern reads — late entries, early exits, and absence patterns (Chapter 7).

The design decision, made before configuration. Decide per location which marking method applies:

1. Auto attendance from checkins — a clock device or the mobile checkin feeds Employee Checkin rows; the Shift Type's settings process them into Attendance records. Use where devices exist and shifts are defined.
2. Manual marking — a responsible person marks the day's attendance with the Employee Attendance Tool. Use where no device exists.
3. Exception-only — attendance records are created only for absences and leave; unmarked days are treated per the Payroll Settings unmarked-attendance rule. Use only with that rule's consequence understood (the Payroll track, module 8, Chapter 2).

Record the decision per location. Chapter 8's worked example applies one method per HealthTrade location.

Module contents. Chapter 2: Holiday Lists. Chapter 3: Attendance records and Employee Checkin. Chapter 4: Shift Type and auto attendance. Chapter 5: Shift Assignment. Chapter 6: manual marking and the Employee Attendance Tool. Chapter 7: Attendance Requests and the standing reads. Chapter 8: worked example. Chapter 9: review and the module rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Holiday List
lessons.html:
Open Holiday List (awesome bar) > New. Build one list per working pattern. Complete the fields in order.

1. Holiday List Name. Name the list for its pattern and year: Standard 2026, Retail Branches 2026 (Sun only). Lists are period-bound; a new year needs new lists.

2. From Date and To Date. The period the list covers — the calendar year or the company's working year.

3. Weekly offs. Use the Add Weekly Holidays action: select the weekly off day(s) and the tool generates one holiday row per occurrence in the period. A standard pattern selects Saturday and Sunday; a six-day retail pattern selects Sunday only. Run the action once per weekly-off day.

4. The holiday rows. Add the public holidays as individual rows: date and description. Enter the national holidays for the year and any company-declared days. Where a public holiday's date is announced late in the year (movable holidays), add the row when the date is announced — the list is maintained, not set-and-forgotten.

5. Company default. On the Company record, set the Default Holiday List. Employees without a per-employee list fall back to the company default. Set the default to the majority pattern and assign the exceptions per employee (module 1, Chapter 4).

What reads the list. Restated from module 1 with the mechanics:

1. Payment days — working days in a payroll period = period days minus this list's days for the employee. A wrong list produces wrong prorations for everyone assigned to it.
2. Leave day counts — a Leave Application spanning a holiday does not count the holiday as leave where the leave type is configured so (module 4, Chapter 2's include-holiday flag).
3. Auto attendance — no attendance is expected on a list day; the Shift Type's holiday behaviour (Chapter 4) reads it.
4. The Monthly Attendance Sheet — list days render as holidays, not absences.

The annual build procedure.

1. In the last month of the year, create the new year's lists: one per working pattern, weekly offs generated, known public holidays entered.
2. Set the Company default to the new standard list.
3. Update the per-employee Holiday List field for employees on non-default patterns — a bulk update via the governed import where headcount warrants.
4. Verify: filter the Employee list by Holiday List and confirm every Active employee carries a current-year list. An employee carrying last year's expired list has no valid working calendar, and prorations and leave counts fail for them.
5. During the year, add announced movable holidays to every list they apply to, on announcement.

Verification per list. Open the saved list and confirm: the period dates correct; the weekly-off rows present for every week; the public holiday rows complete against the official calendar; no duplicate rows.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Attendance records and Employee Checkin
lessons.html:
This chapter covers the two record types at attendance's core: the raw checkin log and the processed attendance record.

1. The Attendance record. Open Attendance (awesome bar) > New (manual creation; auto attendance and the tool create records the same shape). Fields:

• Employee and Attendance Date — one record per employee per date. The system rejects duplicates for the same employee and date.
• Status — Present, Absent, On Leave, Half Day, or Work From Home. On Leave records are created by approved Leave Applications (module 4); do not create them manually.
• Shift — the shift the record belongs to, where shifts are in use.
• Late Entry and Early Exit — flags set by auto attendance where the checkin times breach the shift's grace settings (Chapter 4); readable on the pattern reports.
• Working Hours — computed from checkins where auto attendance runs.

Attendance records are submittable documents. Corrections follow document rules: cancel and re-create, or the Attendance Request lane (Chapter 7). Do not edit submitted attendance directly.

2. The Employee Checkin record. Open Employee Checkin (awesome bar) — normally read, not created by hand. Fields per row:

• Employee, Time, and Log Type (IN or OUT).
• Device ID — the source device where a biometric or door device feeds the log through its integration.
• Rows also arrive from the mobile checkin feature where the business enables it for field staff.

The checkin sources, configured once.

1. Device integration — the biometric or card device pushes events into Employee Checkin through the integration the sysadmin registers (the Sysadmin track, module 6: the integration register, a dedicated integration user, the credential under custody, and a health check — the device that silently stops pushing is the failure mode; the health check is the day's row count present).
2. Mobile checkin — enabled per the business's policy for staff who work outside a fixed location; the row carries the timestamp and, where configured, the location.
3. Manual checkin entry — the exception lane for a failed device day, entered by the responsible person with a remark. Manual rows are the correction of last resort; the Attendance Request (Chapter 7) is the governed lane for individual missed punches.

The relationship, stated precisely. Checkins are evidence; Attendance is the ruling. Auto attendance (Chapter 4) reads the day's checkins per employee, applies the Shift Type's settings, and writes one Attendance record with the computed status, hours, and flags. Nothing reads checkins directly for pay; everything reads the Attendance records they produce. A dispute about a day is settled by opening both: the checkin rows (what the device recorded) and the Attendance record (what the settings concluded), with the Attendance Request lane carrying any correction.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The Shift Type and auto attendance
lessons.html:
Open Shift Type (awesome bar) > New. The Shift Type defines the working hours and carries the auto-attendance settings. Complete the fields in order; the auto-attendance block is this module's most consequential configuration.

1. Name, Start Time, End Time. Name the shift for its pattern: Head Office 08:00-17:00, Warehouse Early 07:00-15:00. Enter the shift's start and end times.

2. Enable Auto Attendance. Tick to have the system create Attendance records from Employee Checkin rows for this shift. The remaining settings govern how.

3. Determine Check-in and Check-out. Two options:

• Alternating entries as IN and OUT — the day's rows alternate: first row IN, second OUT, third IN, fourth OUT. Use where staff punch at every entry and exit (breaks included) and working hours should sum the intervals.
• Strictly based on Log Type — the rows' own IN/OUT types are used; typically read as first IN and last OUT. Use where the device records log types reliably and hours should span first arrival to last departure.

Choose per device behaviour and record the choice; the working-hours figures differ materially between the two.

4. Working Hours Calculation Based On — first check-in and last check-out, or every valid check-in/check-out pair. Pairs with the setting above.

5. The thresholds.

• Working Hours Threshold for Half Day — computed hours below this value mark the day Half Day.
• Working Hours Threshold for Absent — computed hours below this value mark the day Absent (a punch-in followed by immediate departure does not earn a Present).

Set both from the business's written attendance policy, not by guess; the thresholds decide pay-affecting statuses.

6. The grace block.

• Enable Entry Grace Period and Late Entry Grace Period (minutes) — a check-in after start time plus grace sets the Late Entry flag.
• Early Exit Grace Period — a check-out before end time minus grace sets the Early Exit flag.

The flags mark, they do not punish: the consequence of accumulated flags is the business's written policy, executed through its own lanes (the pattern read in Chapter 7 produces the data).

7. The window settings. Begin Check-in Before Shift Start Time and Allow Check-out After Shift End Time (minutes) — the window inside which checkins attach to this shift. Size the windows to the real arrival spread; a checkin outside the window attaches to no shift and produces no attendance, which surfaces as an unexplained Absent.

8. Process Attendance After — the date auto attendance begins processing for this shift. Set to the go-live date; do not leave it in the past on a new shift or the processor attempts historical days with no checkins.

9. Last Sync of Checkin. The timestamp up to which checkin data is considered complete. Auto attendance marks Absent for missing checkins only up to this timestamp. Where a device pushes on a schedule, this field advances with the pushes; where it stalls, attendance processing stalls with it. The daily read (Chapter 7) includes this field: a Last Sync older than the device's push schedule is the device-integration failure surfacing.

Verification after configuration. Run one test cycle: two test checkins for one employee inside the window; confirm the created Attendance record's status, hours, and flags match the settings' intent; repeat with a late check-in and confirm the flag. Record the test in the configuration note.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The Shift Assignment
lessons.html:
A Shift Type applies to an employee through a Shift Assignment. This chapter covers assignment, defaults, and changes.

1. The default shift. The Employee record carries a Default Shift field; where a stable pattern applies, set it there and the employee's checkins process against that shift without per-period assignments. Use the default for fixed-pattern staff (head office on one shift permanently).

2. The Shift Assignment record. Open Shift Assignment (awesome bar) > New:

• Employee and Shift Type.
• Start Date and End Date — the period the assignment governs. An open End Date runs until superseded.
• Status — Active or Inactive.

Use assignments where patterns vary: rotating warehouse shifts, temporary cover on a different shift, a branch moving patterns for a season. The assignment with dates overrides the default shift for its period; auto attendance reads the applicable shift per day from the assignment calendar.

3. Rotation procedure. For rotating patterns, create the period's assignments in advance from the rota:

1. The rota is decided by the responsible manager and documented.
2. Assignments are entered per employee per rotation block (the governed import where volume warrants).
3. Verify coverage: filter Shift Assignment by period and confirm every rotating employee has an assignment for every working day of the period. A gap day has no shift, and the day's checkins attach to nothing — the unexplained-Absent failure from Chapter 4 restated at the assignment layer.

4. The Shift Request. Where the site enables employee-initiated shift requests, the Shift Request document carries the employee's request for a shift or period, routed to approval; an approved request creates the assignment. Where the business schedules top-down only, the feature stays unused and shifts enter as assignments per the rota — decide once and record which lane the business uses.

5. Changing shifts. A pattern change is a new assignment from its date; the old assignment ends the day before. Do not edit a past assignment's dates to reshape history — past attendance was processed against the shifts as they stood, and the standing rule applies: history stands, changes go forward with honest dates.

The assignment reads.

1. The coverage read — before each period: every rotating employee assigned for every working day (step 3 above).
2. The orphan read — monthly: Active employees on checkin-based locations with neither a Default Shift nor a current assignment. Every name on this list is producing checkins that process against nothing.
3. The alignment read — where a location changes its hours, the Shift Type is updated (or a successor created) and the assignments confirmed — a device pushing checkins against a shift whose times no longer match the door's reality flags every worker late every day, which surfaces in Chapter 7's pattern read as a whole location turning red at once.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Manual marking and the Employee Attendance Tool
lessons.html:
Locations without checkin devices mark attendance manually. This chapter covers the tool, the procedure, and the controls.

1. The Employee Attendance Tool. Open Employee Attendance Tool (awesome bar). The tool marks attendance in bulk:

1. Select the Date.
2. Filter by Department or Branch to load the location's employees.
3. The tool lists the employees not yet marked for the date; employees with existing records (an approved leave's On Leave record, an auto-attendance record) do not appear — the tool does not overwrite.
4. Select the employees and mark the status: Present, Absent, or Half Day. Marked employees receive Attendance records for the date.

2. The daily marking procedure, per manual location.

1. The responsible person (named per location — the branch manager or their deputy) marks the day's attendance at a fixed time (end of day, or the following morning per the location's written procedure).
2. Absences are marked Absent only when no leave record covers them; a known approved leave shows as On Leave already (module 4 posts it). An absence that should be leave is routed to the leave lane, not marked around.
3. Half days are marked per the policy's definition.
4. The marking is complete when the tool's unmarked list for the date and location is empty.

3. The unmarked-day control. An unmarked day is the manual method's failure mode, and it has a pay consequence: the Payroll Settings unmarked-attendance rule (the Payroll track, module 8, Chapter 2) decides what an unmarked day means at payroll — and both settings of that rule are wrong for someone when marking is incomplete. The control is a read, not a hope:

1. Weekly: the Monthly Attendance Sheet (Chapter 7) for the week, per manual location — gaps in the grid are unmarked days, closed by the responsible person while the week is current and memory is reliable.
2. At the records close (the Payroll track, module 3, Station 1): the month's attendance complete for every manual location, confirmed as a checklist line. Attendance completed after the close takes the payroll correction lane, which is the incentive to complete it before.

4. Marking discipline.

1. The marker marks from observation or the location's register, not from recollection days later — hence the fixed daily time.
2. The marker does not mark their own attendance status exceptions; their own corrections route through the Attendance Request lane like anyone else's (Chapter 7).
3. Bulk historical marking (a location discovered unmarked for weeks) is an incident: marked from the best contemporaneous evidence, noted as reconstructed, and the cause — the procedure that lapsed — fixed per the standing incident discipline.

5. Mixed sites. A business can run auto attendance at devices locations and manual marking elsewhere; the Attendance records are identical downstream. The per-location method decision (Chapter 1) and the per-location responsible names are the configuration; the reads in Chapter 7 cover both methods in one grid.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Attendance Requests and the standing reads
lessons.html:
This chapter covers the correction lane and the reads that keep attendance reliable.

1. The Attendance Request. Open Attendance Request (awesome bar) > New — the governed lane for attendance corrections and exceptional statuses:

• Employee, From Date, To Date — the day or span.
• Reason — the categories per the site's configuration: the missed punch (present but the device shows no checkin), Work From Home where the policy allows it, on-duty absence (the employee at a supplier or branch on assignment).
• Explanation — the request's account, with evidence where the policy asks it.

The request routes to approval per the routing design (module 1, Chapter 7). An approved request creates or corrects the Attendance records for its span. The lane's purpose: no attendance status changes on a conversation — the missed punch that becomes a Present has a document with an approver, and the pattern read below includes request frequency per employee (a monthly missed punch is a device problem or a habit; the data distinguishes them).

2. The daily read (auto-attendance locations). Thirty seconds per location:

1. Last Sync of Checkin current against the device's push schedule (Chapter 4's field) — a stale sync is the device integration failing; raise per the integration's register entry.
2. Yesterday's checkin row count plausible for the location's headcount — a zero-row day at a working location is the same failure seen from the data side.

3. The weekly read. The Monthly Attendance Sheet report (awesome bar), filtered to the week and location:

1. The grid per employee per day: statuses, holidays rendering as holidays.
2. Gaps (unmarked days) closed per Chapter 6's control.
3. Unexplained Absents investigated while the week is current: the checkin rows opened for the day (a window or assignment gap from Chapters 4-5 shows as checkins with no attendance), the correction routed through the request lane.

4. The monthly reads (with the records close).

1. Completeness: the month's sheet gap-free for every location; the payroll checklist line confirmed.
2. The pattern read: Late Entry and Early Exit flags summarised per employee and location; absence counts summarised. The output is data to the responsible managers per the written policy — the module produces the read; the consequences belong to the policy's owners. A location-wide flag spike is checked against Chapter 5's alignment read (shift times versus reality) before any conversation about individuals.
3. The request-lane read: Attendance Requests by employee and reason for the month — device-problem clusters routed to the integration owner; policy questions to the policy owner.

5. The payroll tie, restated. Whichever payroll basis the site runs (the Payroll Settings decision), the meeting point is the records close: leave recorded (module 4), attendance complete (this module), by the close date — the Payroll track's Station 1, line 4 assumes both. The run-two case in the Payroll track's module 3 (an absence never entered, caught at the register comparison) is the failure this module's completeness reads prevent at source.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: HealthTrade attendance
lessons.html:
This chapter applies Chapters 2-7 to HealthTrade. Configuration values and outcomes are listed per step.

Step 1 — Holiday Lists (Chapter 2). Two lists built for the year: Standard 2026 (weekly offs Saturday and Sunday, generated by the Add Weekly Holidays action; the year's public holidays entered) and Retail Branches 2026 (Sunday only; same public holidays). Company Default Holiday List set to Standard 2026; the three branches' retail and warehouse staff assigned the branch list per employee (module 1's field). Verification: the Employee list filtered by Holiday List shows every Active employee on a current-year list.

Step 2 — the method decision (Chapter 1). Recorded per location: Central Lagos warehouse — auto attendance (a biometric device exists); Head Office — auto attendance (door device); Ibadan and Akure branches — manual marking (no devices; the branch managers named as markers, end-of-day marking time set).

Step 3 — Shift Types (Chapter 4). Three shifts configured: Head Office 08:00-17:00, Warehouse Early 07:00-15:00, Warehouse Late 11:00-19:00. Auto attendance enabled on all three; determination set to Strictly based on Log Type (the devices record IN/OUT reliably); thresholds set from the written policy (half day below five hours; absent below two); grace periods fifteen minutes entry and exit; windows sixty minutes before start and after end; Process Attendance After set to the go-live date. The test cycle runs per shift: two test checkins, the created record's status and hours confirmed; one deliberate late check-in confirms the Late Entry flag.

Step 4 — assignments (Chapter 5). Head office staff receive Default Shift on the Employee record (fixed pattern). Warehouse staff rotate weekly between Early and Late: the month's rota entered as Shift Assignments via the governed import; the coverage read confirms every rotating employee assigned for every working day.

Step 5 — the device integration (Chapter 3). The biometric integrations registered per the Sysadmin track's procedure: dedicated integration users, credentials in custody, the health check defined as the daily row count. The daily read (Last Sync current, row count plausible) joins the standing calendar.

Step 6 — month one findings. Listed flat, each with its correction:

1. Six warehouse checkins on day three attached to no shift — punches earlier than the sixty-minute window on the Early shift. Window widened to ninety minutes before start; the six days corrected through Attendance Requests.
2. One Head Office employee showing Absent on two days with checkin rows present — no Default Shift set on a new joiner's record; the field completed, the days corrected via requests. The orphan read added to the monthly list to catch this class before it produces Absents.
3. The Ibadan sheet showing four unmarked days in week two — the marker was on leave and no deputy was named; a deputy named per location, the days closed from the branch register while current.
4. The pattern read's first month: Late Entry flags concentrated on the Warehouse Late shift's Mondays — checked against the alignment read first (shift times correct), then handed as data to the operations manager per the policy.

Result. Two lists, three shifts, two device integrations with health checks, one manual-marking procedure with named markers and deputies, and a month-one findings list of four items, all corrected through the lanes. The records close for the month confirms attendance complete at every location; the payroll run's payment-days figures compute without manual intervention.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common errors and the module rule
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in attendance, each with its correction and prevention.

Error 1 — the stale sync. Symptom: attendance processing stopped; Absents accumulating for present staff; Last Sync of Checkin days old. Correction: the device integration restored per its register entry; the affected days reprocessed or corrected through requests. Prevention: the daily read — Last Sync against the push schedule, row count against headcount.

Error 2 — the window and assignment gaps. Symptom: checkin rows present, Attendance absent — punches outside the shift window, or days with no applicable shift (assignment gaps, missing Default Shift). Correction: the window resized or the assignment/default completed; the days corrected via Attendance Requests. Prevention: windows sized to real arrival spread at configuration; the coverage and orphan reads run per period.

Error 3 — guessed thresholds and grace. Symptom: Half Day and Absent statuses, and Late flags, disputed because the numbers behind them were never policy. Correction: the thresholds and grace set from the written attendance policy; disputed days re-examined against checkins. Prevention: the policy written before the Shift Type is configured; the settings recorded with their policy reference.

Error 4 — the unmarked manual location. Symptom: grid gaps at manual locations; the payroll unmarked-attendance rule producing wrong payment days in one direction or the other. Correction: the days closed from contemporaneous evidence, noted as reconstructed where late. Prevention: named markers with deputies, the fixed daily marking time, the weekly gap read, and the records-close completeness line.

Error 5 — corrections by conversation. Symptom: attendance statuses changed on request without documents; no trail of who approved the missed-punch Present. Correction: the changes re-documented through Attendance Requests where still possible. Prevention: the request lane as the only correction path, and the monthly request-lane read distinguishing device problems from habits.

Error 6 — history reshaped. Symptom: past Shift Assignments' dates edited to fit a new rota; past attendance no longer matching the shifts it was processed against. Correction: the edits reversed; changes re-entered as new assignments from honest dates. Prevention: the standing rule — history stands; pattern changes are new assignments forward.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: state the four record types and their relationship, and the three marking methods with the per-location decision; build a Holiday List with weekly offs and public holidays and run the annual build procedure; read Attendance and Employee Checkin records and state the checkin sources; configure a Shift Type's auto-attendance block — determination, thresholds, grace, windows, Process Attendance After, Last Sync — and run the test cycle; assign shifts by default and by Shift Assignment with the coverage, orphan, and alignment reads; run manual marking with the Employee Attendance Tool and the unmarked-day controls; and operate the Attendance Request lane with the daily, weekly, and monthly reads.

Module rule 3: attendance is recorded per day per employee — checkins as evidence, the Shift Type's settings as the ruling, manual locations marked daily by named people, corrections through the request lane, and the month complete at the records close. Module 4 covers leave management.

leave.title: HR 4 — Leave Management
leave.desc: Leave in ZhiftERP: the five-record dependency order; the Leave Type's twelve behaviour flags configured from the written policy with the type register; Leave Period, Leave Policy, and the Leave Policy Assignment generating allocations in the annual round with its completeness verification; Leave Allocation mechanics including carry-forward caps and the lawful manual cases; the Leave Application workflow — computed day counts, approver reads, the records-close rule, blocked-application diagnosis; Leave Without Pay with its payment-days consequence; compensatory leave earned on evidence and in-service encashment on the policy line; and the Employee Leave Balance report with the leave ledger.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Leave management: scope and record structure
lessons.html:
This module covers leave in ZhiftERP. On completing this module you will be able to: configure Leave Types with their behaviour flags; create Leave Periods; build Leave Policies and apply them through Leave Policy Assignments; create and read Leave Allocations; process Leave Applications through the approval workflow; operate leave without pay with its payroll consequence; run compensatory leave; and read balances through the leave reports.

The record structure. Leave uses five record types in a strict dependency order:

1. Leave Type — the definition of one kind of leave and its rules (Chapter 2). Built first.
2. Leave Period — the dated container, normally the leave year (Chapter 3).
3. Leave Policy — the entitlement package: which types, how many days each, per employee group (Chapter 3).
4. Leave Allocation — the record that gives one employee a balance of one type for a period (Chapter 4). Created in bulk by the Leave Policy Assignment or manually.
5. Leave Application — one employee's request to use allocated days, through approval to posted attendance (Chapter 5).

The dependency is absolute: an application checks its allocation; an allocation belongs to a period; the policy generates allocations from types. Configure in this order.

What reads leave.

1. Attendance — an approved application posts On Leave attendance for its days (module 3).
2. Payroll — leave without pay reduces payment days (the Payroll track, module 1, Chapter 6); where the payroll basis is leave, all absence enters through leave records. The records-close date (the Payroll track, module 3) is the deadline by which the month's leave is entered and approved.
3. The exit — the leave balance at the relieving date feeds encashment (the Payroll track, module 7, Chapter 3). The balance is trustworthy at exit only if it was maintained all year; this module is where it is maintained.
4. The slip — where Payroll Settings shows leave balances on salary slips (the Payroll track, module 8, Chapter 2), the figures shown are this module's balances.

Custody. HR configures the machinery and administers allocations; employees apply; the approvers named in the routing design (module 1) approve; the leave policy itself — entitlements, rules, encashment terms — is the business's written policy, decided by the owner and recorded before configuration. The standing rule applies: the configuration states what the policy states.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the Leave Type and its flags. Chapter 3: Leave Period, Leave Policy, and the Policy Assignment. Chapter 4: the Leave Allocation. Chapter 5: the Leave Application and approval. Chapter 6: leave without pay. Chapter 7: compensatory leave and encashment in service. Chapter 8: the balance reads. Chapter 9: worked example. Chapter 10: review and the module rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Leave Type
lessons.html:
Open Leave Type (awesome bar) > New. One record per kind of leave. The flags on this doctype define the type's entire behaviour; walk them in order and set each from the written policy.

1. Leave Type Name. Plain names: Annual Leave, Sick Leave, Casual Leave, Leave Without Pay, Compensatory Leave, Maternity Leave.

2. Max Leaves Allowed. The ceiling on allocation for this type per period. The policy's annual entitlement figures are entered on the Leave Policy (Chapter 3); this field caps them.

3. Applicable After (Working Days). The qualifying period: the type cannot be applied for until the employee has completed this many working days from joining. Use for entitlements that start after probation.

4. Maximum Continuous Days Allowed. The longest single application for this type. Applications beyond it are blocked; longer absences per policy route to the appropriate type or an exception decision.

5. Is Carry Forward. Ticked, unused balance can carry into the next period's allocation, up to the configured carry-forward cap. Clear, the balance lapses at period end. Set per the policy's carry rule; Chapter 4 covers the mechanics at allocation time.

6. Is Leave Without Pay. Ticked, days of this type reduce payment days at payroll. This flag is the payroll tie: exactly one type (named Leave Without Pay) normally carries it, and Chapter 6 covers its operation. Paid leave types leave it clear.

7. Allow Negative Balance. Ticked, applications can exceed the allocated balance. Leave it clear as the default: a negative balance is unearned paid absence, and where the policy genuinely permits borrowing against future allocation, the permission is a written policy line and the flag is set with that reference recorded.

8. Include Holiday within Leaves as Leaves. Ticked, holidays inside an application's span consume balance; clear, they do not (the Holiday List interaction — module 3, Chapter 2). The common configuration is clear: a Friday-to-Monday application over a weekend consumes two days, not four. Set per policy and state the rule to staff, because the day count on the application form follows it.

9. Is Optional Leave. For optional-holiday schemes: the type draws from a published list of optional holidays from which employees choose a limited number. Used with the optional Holiday List the scheme defines; unused where the business has no such scheme.

10. Is Compensatory. Ticked, allocations of this type are created by approved Compensatory Leave Requests (Chapter 7) — days earned by working on holidays, not granted by policy allocation.

11. Allow Encashment. Ticked, the type participates in Leave Encashment (in-service per policy — Chapter 7 — and at exit per the Payroll track, module 7). The encashment rate basis is configured with the salary structure per that track.

12. Is Earned Leave, Earn Leave Frequency, Rounding. For accrual schemes: the entitlement accrues per period (monthly or quarterly) rather than granting in full at allocation. The allocation is created for the period and the balance grows by the earned amount per frequency, rounded per the rounding setting. Use where the policy accrues; grant-in-full policies leave it clear.

Verification. After building the types, produce the one-page type register: each type, its flags, and the policy line that set each flag. The register is read at the annual policy review and answers every question of why a type behaves as it does from configuration, not recollection.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Leave Period, Leave Policy, and the Policy Assignment
lessons.html:
Three records turn types into entitlements. Build them in order.

1. The Leave Period. Open Leave Period (awesome bar) > New: the company, the From Date and To Date — normally the leave year (the calendar year, or the business's leave year where it differs). Allocations belong to a period; applications consume balances inside their period. Create the new period before the year turns; the annual procedure in Chapter 4 depends on it existing.

2. The Leave Policy. Open Leave Policy > New. The policy is the entitlement package:

• The Leave Policy Details table — one row per leave type with its Annual Allocation: Annual Leave 15, Sick Leave 10, Casual Leave 5, per the written policy. Leave Without Pay is not allocated (it is unlimited by allocation and governed by approval — Chapter 6); compensatory leave is not allocated by policy (it is earned — Chapter 7).
• Submit the policy. Policies are versioned by the document rules: a changed entitlement is a new policy or amendment from its effective period, not an edit that rewrites what past allocations were generated from.

Build one policy per genuinely different entitlement package: a single company-wide policy where entitlements are uniform; separate policies where they differ by category (the contract-staff policy with different figures — the Employment Type distinction from module 1 becoming a policy boundary).

3. The Leave Policy Assignment. Open Leave Policy Assignment > New — the record that applies a policy to employees for a period:

• The Employee (or the bulk lane below), the Leave Policy, and the Leave Period (or explicit dates).
• On submission, the assignment creates the Leave Allocations: one allocation per policy row per employee, dated to the period. This is the bulk mechanism: the annual entitlement round is policy assignments, not hand-made allocations.
• The bulk lane: assignments created for a set of employees (by grade, department, or the full list per the site's tooling, or via the governed import) in one pass at period start.

The annual entitlement procedure.

1. The new Leave Period created (step 1).
2. The policy confirmed against the written policy for the new year — changes enter as new policy versions.
3. Policy Assignments created for all Active employees against the new period — the allocations generate.
4. Carry-forward processed where types allow it (Chapter 4's mechanics).
5. Verification: the allocation count equals Active employees × policy rows; the exceptions (joiners mid-period, category differences) reconciled by name. An employee without a new-period allocation cannot apply for leave in the new year, and the failure surfaces as blocked applications in January — the verification prevents it in December.

Mid-year joiners. A joiner receives their policy assignment at onboarding (the onboarding template's HR activity — module 2, Chapter 7): the assignment against the current period, with the allocation prorated per the policy's joining rule (the proration entered on the allocation per Chapter 4, from the policy's stated arithmetic).

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The Leave Allocation
lessons.html:
Open Leave Allocation (awesome bar). One allocation gives one employee a balance of one leave type for one span. Most allocations are generated by Policy Assignments (Chapter 3); this chapter covers the record itself, manual creation, carry-forward, and the allocation reads.

1. The record's fields.

• Employee, Leave Type, From Date, To Date — the who, what, and span (normally the leave period's dates).
• New Leaves Allocated — the days granted for the span.
• Carry Forward — ticked, the allocation adds the unused balance from the previous period's allocation of the same type, up to the type's carry-forward cap. The total balance = carried days + new leaves allocated.
• Allocations are submittable; corrections follow document rules.

2. Manual allocation — the lawful cases.

1. The prorated joiner — the mid-year joiner's allocation at the policy's prorated figure, arithmetic per the written policy (months remaining ÷ 12 × annual figure, rounded per policy), entered with the computation in the remark.
2. The policy exception — an individually agreed entitlement (a negotiated extra week, documented in the employee's terms): allocated manually with the agreement attached. The standing rule applies — no allocation without its documented decision.
3. The correction — an allocation error fixed by cancel/amend with the cause noted.

Everything else comes from Policy Assignments. A register of hand-made allocations that should have been policy-generated is the leave equivalent of the structure-per-person error: fold the pattern back into a policy.

3. Carry-forward at the period turn. Run with the annual procedure (Chapter 3):

1. For each carry-forward type, the new period's allocations are created with Carry Forward ticked — the system computes the carried balance per employee up to the cap.
2. Verify a sample: an employee's closing balance last period versus their carried figure this period, against the cap. The cap is the policy's number; balances above it lapse, and the lapse is the policy working, not an error — state it in the staff communication at year turn so the December applications surge is informed rather than surprised.
3. Non-carry types simply end; their new allocations grant fresh.

4. The allocation reads.

1. The completeness read (annual, from Chapter 3's verification): Active employees × policy rows = allocations, exceptions named.
2. The balance integrity read (quarterly): the Employee Leave Balance report (Chapter 8) sampled against the ledger — allocations minus approved applications = balance, per the leave ledger entries the system keeps. A balance that does not reconcile is a cancelled-document or manual-entry artefact, investigated through the ledger.
3. The negative-balance read (monthly, where any type allows negatives): every negative balance listed with its authorising policy line — a negative on a type that does not allow negatives is a configuration change to investigate.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The Leave Application and the approval workflow
lessons.html:
Open Leave Application (awesome bar) > New — or receive applications through employee self-service, which is the standard lane. This chapter covers the form, the workflow, and the administration rules.

1. The form's fields.

• Employee — self-filled through self-service; the applicant applies for themselves.
• Leave Type — the type being consumed. The form shows the leave balance for the selected type as of the application — the applicant sees what they hold before applying.
• From Date, To Date, Half Day — the span; the half-day flag with its date where the policy allows half days.
• Total Leave Days — computed by the system: the span's days minus holidays per the type's include-holiday flag (Chapter 2) and the employee's Holiday List (module 3). The computed figure is the figure that will consume balance; the applicant and approver both read it.
• Reason — the applicant's statement.
• Leave Approver — resolved per the routing design (module 1, Chapter 7): the department's leave approver table or the per-employee field.

2. The workflow. Status Open on submission by the applicant → the approver's action:

1. Approved — on submission of the approval: the balance is consumed, and On Leave attendance records post for the span's working days (module 3's third creation path). The application is the document; the attendance is its effect.
2. Rejected — with the reason recorded; the balance is untouched.
3. Cancellation of an approved application (plans changed) reverses its balance consumption and its attendance records per document rules — cancel the document, never hand-edit balances or attendance.

3. The approver's read, per application.

1. The balance covers the days (the form shows both).
2. The dates against the team's calendar (the operational judgment the approver holds).
3. The type appropriate to the reason per policy (sick leave with the policy's evidence rule where the span triggers it; the evidence attached to the application).
4. The decision made in the system, not in conversation-then-system-later: the application's status is the decision, and module 3's records-close discipline needs it entered by the close.

4. Administration rules.

1. Applications precede absence where the absence is plannable; unplanned absence (sickness) is applied for on return or during, per policy, with the span honest — the application dated to the actual absence, never adjusted to fit balances.
2. The records-close tie: the month's leave applications entered and decided by the payroll records close (the Payroll track, module 3, Station 1, line 4). Pending applications at the close are decided or the affected days handled per the unmarked rules — the run-two case in the Payroll track (an absence entered nowhere, caught at the register comparison) is the failure this rule prevents at source: absence enters through this module's records, by the close, every month.
3. No proxy applications: the employee applies through their own login; where genuine incapacity prevents it, HR enters on the employee's behalf with the authority noted — an application entered by another hand without a note is an access finding (the Sysadmin track's individual-credential rule).
4. The blocked-application diagnosis: an application the system refuses is read against its dependency chain — no allocation for the period (Chapter 3's completeness failure), the qualifying period unmet (the Applicable After setting), the continuous-days cap, or the negative-balance rule. The refusal names the rule; the fix is the record or the policy conversation, never an override entered around it.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Leave without pay
lessons.html:
Leave Without Pay (LWP) is the leave type whose days reduce pay. This chapter covers its configuration, its lane, and its payroll consequence.

1. Configuration. One Leave Type named Leave Without Pay with Is Leave Without Pay ticked (Chapter 2, flag 6). No allocation: LWP is not an entitlement with a balance; it is an approval-governed state. The type's other flags per policy — the continuous-days cap where the policy limits single spans, the include-holiday flag consistent with the paid types.

2. When LWP applies. Per the written policy, the standing cases:

1. Paid entitlements exhausted and further absence approved — the applicant's Annual and Casual balances at zero, the absence genuine, the approval given as LWP.
2. Absence categories the policy defines as unpaid from the first day (the policy's own list — extended personal leave, study leave where unpaid, and the business's other defined cases).
3. Unauthorised absence converted per policy: an absence with no application and no acceptable account is handled per the disciplinary policy, and where that policy's outcome is unpaid status for the days, the LWP application records it with the decision attached — the pay consequence executes through the record, not through a quiet payroll adjustment (the Payroll track's written-decision rule).

3. The lane. LWP travels the same Leave Application workflow (Chapter 5): applied (or entered by HR with authority noted, per the policy case), routed to the approver, approved with the decision documented. The approval bar is the policy's: LWP is a pay-affecting decision and its approver is named accordingly in the routing design.

4. The payroll consequence, mechanically. An approved LWP application posts its days; at payroll, the payment-days computation (the Payroll track, module 1, Chapter 6) subtracts LWP days from working days, and every component with Depends on Payment Days pays its reduced fraction. Verification points:

1. The slip's payment-days figure for an LWP month equals working days minus the approved LWP days — the payroll draft review's spot-check (its module 3, Station 3) holds the LWP list against the slips.
2. The employee's payday explanation is prepared: the application, the day count, the arithmetic (the Payroll track, module 4's standing answers — the proration answer's LWP case).

5. The records-close rule, restated for LWP. LWP is the leave record with the largest pay consequence, and the month's LWP must be entered and approved by the records close. The cross-track case: the Payroll track's module 3 run-two finding — a warehouse assistant's four unpaid days entered nowhere, caught only at the register comparison — had its cause in leave submissions arriving by message instead of through this module. The fix lives here: absence enters as Leave Applications through the system, by the close, and the branch procedure names who enters what by when.

6. The LWP reads. Monthly: the month's LWP days by employee and branch, tied to the payroll spot-check list. Quarterly: the LWP pattern — repeated LWP on exhausted balances is data for the policy owner (an entitlement sized wrong, or an attendance matter), presented per the standing data-not-editorial rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Compensatory leave and in-service encashment
lessons.html:
Two special flows on the standard machinery.

1. Compensatory leave. Days earned by working on holidays, taken later as leave. The records:

1. The Leave Type — Compensatory Leave with Is Compensatory ticked (Chapter 2, flag 10). No policy allocation; the balance is earned.
2. The Compensatory Leave Request (awesome bar > New) — the earning document: the employee, the work date(s) (which must be holidays on the employee's Holiday List, with attendance evidence per the site — the checkin rows or marked attendance for the day), and the reason. Routed to approval.
3. On approval, the allocation creates — the earned day(s) added to the employee's Compensatory Leave balance, with the expiry the configuration sets (compensatory balances commonly expire per policy; the expiry is stated to the employee at approval).
4. Consumption — a standard Leave Application against the Compensatory type (Chapter 5's workflow unchanged).

The control: the request's work date verified against the Holiday List and the attendance evidence before approval — compensatory leave is earned by documented holiday work, and the request without evidence is returned, not approved on recollection. The quarterly read: compensatory earnings by location — a location earning compensatory days every weekend has a staffing pattern the operations owner should see as data.

2. In-service encashment. Where the written policy allows encashing part of the balance during service (distinct from the exit encashment the Payroll track, module 7 covers):

1. The policy line first — which types (Allow Encashment ticked — Chapter 2, flag 11), how many days per period, when in the year, at what rate basis. No line, no encashment.
2. The Leave Encashment record — the same doctype as at exit: employee, leave type, period; the balance pulled; the encashable days per the policy's cap; the amount computed at the configured rate basis.
3. The payment — through payroll as a documented earning (the encashment lands on the slip per the configuration), taxed per the accountant's ruling on encashment (the Payroll track, module 7, Chapter 3's ruling applies in service as at exit).
4. The balance consumes — encashed days leave the balance; the leave ledger records the encashment entry.

The verification: the encashment's arithmetic on its record (days × rate basis = amount), the policy cap respected, and the payroll month's register carrying the encashment line against the record. The annual read: encashment days and amounts by type — fed to the policy review beside the carry-forward lapse figures, because the two numbers together describe whether the entitlement is sized to how the staff actually rest, which is the policy owner's question to answer.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — The balance reads and the leave ledger
lessons.html:
Every balance question is answered from two instruments. This chapter covers both and the standing reads built on them.

1. The Employee Leave Balance report. Open Employee Leave Balance (awesome bar). The report shows, per employee per leave type for the selected period: the opening (allocated + carried), the used, and the closing balance. Filters: company, period, employee, department. This is the standing balance instrument:

• The individual lookup — an employee's balances in one row set; the answer to "how many days do I have" (also visible to the employee on their own application form and, where configured, their salary slip — the self-answer lanes that reduce lookup traffic).
• The management view — balances by department before peak season; high balances flagged to managers where the policy wants leave taken rather than accumulated (the data-not-editorial rule: the read shows the balances; the taking-leave conversation is the manager's).

2. The leave ledger. Every balance movement writes a leave ledger entry: allocations (positive), applications (negative on approval), encashments, expiries, carry-forwards. The ledger is the audit trail behind the report's figures:

• The reconciliation read (Chapter 4's quarterly integrity read): a sampled employee's report balance recomputed from their ledger entries — allocation minus approved applications minus encashments equals the closing figure. A mismatch is investigated through the ledger's entries, and its cause is a document event (a cancellation, a manual entry) found by reading, not guessing.
• The dispute answer — an employee disputing their balance is answered by their ledger: every movement, dated, with its document. The conversation is a walk through records.

3. The standing reads, by cadence.

1. Monthly (with the records close): the month's applications all decided (no Open applications spanning the closed month); the LWP list to the payroll spot-check (Chapter 6); the negative-balance read where applicable (Chapter 4).
2. Quarterly: the ledger reconciliation sample; the compensatory-earnings read (Chapter 7); the balance distribution to managers ahead of peak seasons.
3. Annually (with the entitlement round): the completeness verification (allocations = employees × rows); the carry-forward and lapse figures; the encashment totals; the type register (Chapter 2) re-read against the written policy — the policy review's data pack is these four numbers per type.

4. The exit tie, restated. The Payroll track's exit chapter confirms the leave balance with the employee at the exit's start and computes encashment from it. That confirmation is quick exactly when this chapter's reads ran all year: the balance the leaver signs is the report's figure, backed by the ledger, and the exit's leave line is a lookup. The alternative — the balance reconstructed at exit from fragmentary records — is the negotiated-balance error the Payroll track lists; its prevention is this module's routine.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Worked example: HealthTrade leave
lessons.html:
This chapter applies Chapters 2-8 to HealthTrade. Configuration values and outcomes are listed per step.

Step 1 — the written policy. Confirmed with the MD before configuration: Annual Leave 15 days, carry-forward allowed up to 5; Sick Leave 10 days, no carry, evidence required beyond 2 continuous days; Casual Leave 5 days, no carry; Leave Without Pay per the approval rules; Compensatory Leave for holiday work, expiring per policy. Holidays inside applications do not consume balance.

Step 2 — Leave Types (Chapter 2). Five types built. Key flags: Annual — Is Carry Forward ticked, Allow Encashment ticked (exit encashment per policy; no in-service encashment line, so none configured); Sick — Applicable After clear (available from joining per policy), no carry; LWP — Is Leave Without Pay ticked, no allocation; Compensatory — Is Compensatory ticked. Include Holiday within Leaves clear on all types per the policy line. The type register written: five types, flags, policy references.

Step 3 — Period, Policy, Assignment (Chapter 3). The 2026 Leave Period created (calendar year). One company-wide Leave Policy: Annual 15, Sick 10, Casual 5. Policy Assignments created for all thirty Active employees in one bulk pass; ninety allocations generate (thirty employees × three policy rows). Verification: count matches; two mid-2025 joiners' prior-period allocations confirmed prorated per the policy arithmetic, computations in the remarks.

Step 4 — the applications go live (Chapter 5). Self-service applications open; the routing runs on the department approver tables (module 1's decision). Month one: eleven applications — nine approved in the system within two days, one rejected (dates against the branch calendar, reason recorded), one cancelled by the applicant. The On Leave attendance posts for every approved span; the Ibadan sheet (module 3's weekly read) shows the leave days as On Leave, not gaps.

Step 5 — the LWP case closed at source (Chapter 6). The branch procedure is issued: absence enters as Leave Applications through the system by the records close; the branch managers enter on behalf only with authority noted. The warehouse assistant's case (the Payroll track's run-two finding — four unpaid days arriving by message and entered nowhere) does not recur: the next occurrence of exhausted-balance absence at Central Lagos enters as an LWP application on day one, approves with the decision attached, posts its days, and the payroll draft review's spot-check finds the slip's payment days already correct — the cross-track fix verified in one cycle.

Step 6 — compensatory and the reads (Chapters 7-8). A stock-count Sunday at Akure produces three Compensatory Leave Requests with checkin evidence; verified against the Holiday List, approved, three one-day allocations created with the expiry stated. The standing reads begin: the monthly close read finds one Open application spanning month-end (decided same day); the quarterly ledger sample reconciles five employees clean; the pre-December balance read to managers flags four staff with 10+ Annual days unused — the taking-leave conversations happen in November, and December's application surge spreads across the quarter instead.

Result. Five types with a written register, ninety allocations generated by one policy assignment pass, self-service applications approving inside the system, LWP entering by the close with the payroll tie verified, compensatory earning on evidence, and the balance instruments answering every lookup. The year-end data pack (carry, lapse, encashment, usage per type) is produced for the first annual policy review.

lessons.title: Chapter 10 — Common errors and the module rule
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in leave management, each with its correction and prevention.

Error 1 — configuration without policy. Symptom: type flags set by guess; entitlements disputed because the configuration answers to nobody's written decision. Correction: the written policy confirmed and the flags reset to it; the type register produced. Prevention: the policy-before-configuration order, and the register's policy-reference column.

Error 2 — the missing allocation. Symptom: blocked applications in the new year; employees who cannot apply because no new-period allocation exists. Correction: the Policy Assignment run for the missed names. Prevention: the annual entitlement procedure in December with its completeness verification (allocations = Active employees × policy rows, exceptions named).

Error 3 — leave outside the system. Symptom: absence agreed by message and entered nowhere; attendance and payroll disagreeing with reality; the register comparison catching what the records never held. Correction: the absent days entered as dated applications with the approvals attached. Prevention: the rule that absence enters as Leave Applications by the records close, with named responsibility per branch — the cross-track fix of Chapter 9, Step 5.

Error 4 — hand-edited balances and attendance. Symptom: balances adjusted directly to fix disputes; On Leave attendance created or deleted by hand; the ledger no longer explaining the report. Correction: the hand edits reversed and the movements re-entered as documents (applications, cancellations, allocations with authority). Prevention: the document-only rule — the ledger records document events, and every balance movement has one.

Error 5 — the negotiated exit balance. Symptom: the leaver's balance disputed at exit; encashment delayed by reconstruction. Correction: the balance rebuilt from the ledger. Prevention: the balance maintained all year by this module's reads — the quarterly ledger sample, the monthly close read — so the exit balance is a lookup the leaver confirms at the exit's start.

Error 6 — compensatory on recollection. Symptom: compensatory days credited without evidence of the holiday work; the earned balance drifting from the worked reality. Correction: pending requests returned for evidence; the credited days sampled against attendance. Prevention: the request verified against the Holiday List and the attendance evidence before approval, every time.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: state the five-record dependency order and what reads leave; configure a Leave Type's twelve flags from the written policy and keep the type register; create the Leave Period, build the Leave Policy, and run the annual Policy Assignment round with its completeness verification; create the lawful manual allocations and process carry-forward with its cap; operate the Leave Application workflow — the computed day count, the approver's four reads, the records-close rule, the blocked-application diagnosis; run LWP with its payroll consequence and verification; operate compensatory leave on evidence and in-service encashment on the policy line; and answer any balance question from the report and the ledger.

Module rule 4: leave is entitlement executed as records — types configured from the written policy, allocations generated by the annual policy round, applications decided in the system by the records close, pay-affecting leave documented like the pay decision it is, and every balance answerable from the ledger. Module 5 covers performance and appraisals.
