performance.title: HR 5 — Performance & Appraisals
performance.desc: Performance management in ZhiftERP: the Appraisal Template with weighted Key Result Areas totalling 100 and rating criteria; the Appraisal Cycle with appraisee-template mapping, the KRA evaluation method decision, and the published calendar; Goal records with KRA links, confirmation, and the freshness discipline; self appraisal and Employee Performance Feedback with independent submission and anchored scales; the final score computed from complete components and corrected only through its records; the completion, freshness, and calibration reads; and the boundary that appraisal informs pay decisions executed through the payroll lanes.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Performance management: scope and record structure
lessons.html:
This module covers performance management in ZhiftERP. On completing this module you will be able to: build Appraisal Templates with weighted Key Result Areas and rating criteria; run an Appraisal Cycle that generates appraisals for its appraisees; track Goals through the period; process self appraisal and Employee Performance Feedback; read the final score computation; and run the cycle's completion and distribution reads.

The record structure. Performance uses five record types:

1. Appraisal Template — the reusable definition of what a role is assessed on: the KRA table with weightages and the rating criteria (Chapter 2). Built once per role family.
2. Appraisal Cycle — the dated container for one assessment round: the period, the appraisee list, and the evaluation settings. Starting the cycle generates the Appraisals (Chapter 3).
3. Appraisal — one employee's assessment for one cycle: the KRA scores, the self appraisal, the feedback, and the final score (Chapters 4-6).
4. Goal — a tracked objective for an employee, linked to a KRA, carrying progress percentage; goals can nest as parent and child (Chapter 4).
5. Employee Performance Feedback — a reviewer's structured feedback against an appraisal, rated on the template's criteria (Chapter 5).

The boundary with pay. Stated before anything is configured: the appraisal record informs pay and promotion decisions; it does not execute them. A pay change that follows an appraisal travels the Payroll track's lanes in full — the approval matrix, the letter, the Salary Structure Assignment (its module 6); a promotion travels module 7's lifecycle documents. The appraisal's final score is an input the deciders read, and the score's arithmetic (this module) must therefore be explainable: weightages recorded, ratings recorded, computation visible on the record.

Custody. HR configures templates and runs cycles; employees maintain goals and submit self appraisals; the named reviewers submit feedback; the deciders decide. The performance policy — what is assessed, how scores are used, the cycle calendar — is the business's written policy, confirmed before configuration per the standing rule.

What reads performance records.

1. The pay review round (the Payroll track, module 6) — final scores as decision inputs.
2. The promotion and transfer documents (module 7) — the appraisal history on the employee.
3. The training-needs read (module 6 of this track) — low-scored KRAs as training-need signals.
4. The cycle reads (Chapter 7) — completion and distribution as management data.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the Appraisal Template. Chapter 3: the Appraisal Cycle. Chapter 4: Goals and the KRA scores. Chapter 5: self appraisal and Employee Performance Feedback. Chapter 6: the final score. Chapter 7: the cycle reads and administration. Chapter 8: worked example. Chapter 9: review and the module rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Appraisal Template
lessons.html:
Open Appraisal Template (awesome bar) > New. One template per role family that is assessed on the same result areas. Complete the fields in order.

1. Template Title. Name the template for its role family: Branch Retail Staff, Warehouse Operations, Management.

2. The KRA table (Key Result Areas). One row per result area the role is assessed on:

• KRA — the result area, from the KRA master (create the KRA records first: short names for assessable result areas — Dispensing accuracy, Stock control, Customer service, Team supervision).
• Weightage (%) — the KRA's share of the score. The weightages must total 100; the document validates the total. Set the weightages from the written performance policy: the weightage is the business's statement of what matters most in the role, and it is decided by the role's manager and the owner, not defaulted to equal splits without a decision.

Rules for the table: three to six KRAs per template (fewer than three assesses too little; more than six dilutes every weightage into noise); each KRA written as an observable result area, not a personality trait — the goal records (Chapter 4) must be able to attach measurable objectives to it.

3. The Rating Criteria table. One row per criterion the reviewers rate on, with its weightage (also totalling 100 where the configuration weights them): the qualitative dimensions the feedback stage assesses — Reliability, Communication, Policy compliance. The criteria rows become the rating rows on every Employee Performance Feedback against appraisals using this template (Chapter 5) — the same structured-comparison design as the recruitment module's Expected Skill Set: every reviewer rates the same rows.

4. Save. The template is reusable across cycles; a role family's template changes through the standing change discipline — a revised template applies to the next cycle, and past appraisals keep the template they were assessed on (history stands).

Template design procedure.

1. The role family's manager drafts the KRAs and weightages from the role's actual duties (the Designation's description — module 1 — is the starting document).
2. The owner confirms the weightages — the 100 points are a decision.
3. HR enters the template and records the decision reference on it.
4. The template is reviewed annually with the performance policy: KRAs that no longer match the role's duties are revised for the next cycle.

Verification. Per template: weightages total 100 in both tables; every KRA exists in the KRA master and is observable; the criteria rows are ratable dimensions; the decision reference recorded.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The Appraisal Cycle
lessons.html:
Open Appraisal Cycle (awesome bar) > New. One cycle per assessment round. Complete the fields in order.

1. Cycle Name, Start Date, End Date. Name the cycle for its round — 2026 Annual, 2026 H1 Probation Reviews — and set the assessment period the cycle covers. Goals and feedback belong to the period; the final scores describe it.

2. Company and the appraisee list. Select the company and build the appraisees table — the employees this cycle assesses. Use the selection tools (department, branch, designation filters) to load groups, then adjust by name. Each appraisee row carries the employee and the Appraisal Template that applies to them — the role-family mapping from Chapter 2 executed here: retail staff to the retail template, warehouse to warehouse, managers to management.

3. The KRA evaluation method. The cycle-level setting that decides how KRA scores compute:

• Automated based on goal progress — each appraisal's KRA score derives from the progress of the Goals linked to that KRA (Chapter 4's mechanics). Use where goals are genuinely maintained through the period.
• Manual rating — the appraiser rates each KRA directly at assessment. Use where the business runs assessment-time rating without period-long goal tracking.

Choose per the written policy and the business's actual discipline — the honest-records rule from the attendance module applies: automated scoring over goals nobody updates produces scores nobody believes. Record the choice on the cycle.

4. The final score formula. Where the configuration exposes the final score weighting (the shares of goal/KRA score, self appraisal, and reviewer feedback in the final figure — Chapter 6), confirm the settings against the policy before the cycle starts. The formula is part of the policy communication to staff: people being assessed are told how the number is built.

5. Create Appraisals. Start the cycle: the system generates one Appraisal per appraisee, each carrying its template's KRA rows. Verify the count — appraisals generated equals appraisee rows — and spot-check three: the right template on the right role.

The cycle calendar. Publish the round's dates when the cycle starts, per the written policy:

1. Cycle start — appraisals generated; goals confirmed (Chapter 4).
2. The period — goals updated as work progresses.
3. Assessment window opens — self appraisals due by a stated date; reviewer feedback due by a stated date.
4. Final scores computed and the calibration read (Chapter 7) run.
5. Outcome conversations held; decision inputs handed to the deciders (the Chapter 1 boundary).

The dates are the cycle's checklist; Chapter 7's completion read tracks submissions against them.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Goals and the KRA scores
lessons.html:
Open Goal (awesome bar) > New — or through employee self-service, the standard lane. Goals carry the period's objectives and, in automated cycles, compute the KRA scores.

1. The Goal record's fields.

• Employee — the goal's owner.
• Goal name — the objective, written as a verifiable outcome: Reduce dispensing errors below two per month, Complete the monthly stock count by the 3rd. A goal whose completion cannot be verified cannot honestly carry a progress figure.
• KRA — the template KRA this goal serves. The link is the scoring path: in automated cycles, a KRA's score derives from its linked goals' progress.
• Appraisal Cycle — the cycle the goal belongs to.
• Start Date / End Date — the goal's own span within the period.
• Progress (%) — the completion figure, updated by the employee as work advances.
• Parent Goal — goals nest: a parent objective with child goals, the parent's progress deriving from its children. Use nesting for large objectives with staged parts; keep the tree shallow (one level of children) or the structure costs more than it informs.

2. Goal setting, at cycle start.

1. The employee drafts goals per KRA — every template KRA carries at least one goal, or that KRA has no scoring basis in an automated cycle.
2. The manager confirms the goals: verifiable, within the role, weighted sensibly across the KRAs. The confirmation is recorded (the manager's comment on the goal or the site's approval step where configured).
3. Mid-period goal changes (a project cancelled, priorities moved by the business) are edits with the manager's confirmation noted — the standing documented-change rule, applied to objectives.

3. Progress discipline.

1. Progress updates are made when the work moves, not reconstructed in the assessment week — the month-end goal read (Chapter 7) lists stale goals (no update in the period's rhythm) as data to managers.
2. Progress states the verifiable position: the figure the evidence supports. The manager's confirmation at assessment (step 4 below) is the check.

4. The KRA score, computed. In an automated cycle: each KRA's score = the progress of its linked goals (averaged or weighted per the configuration), scaled by the KRA's template weightage into the appraisal's goal score. At the assessment window the manager reviews the goals behind each KRA before the score stands — a 100% progress claim on an unverifiable goal is returned for evidence, exactly as any figure without a record is returned anywhere else in the programme.

5. Manual-rating cycles. Where the cycle's method is manual, the appraiser rates each KRA on the appraisal directly at assessment, informed by whatever period evidence exists. Goals remain available as working records even in manual cycles; they simply do not compute the score. The rating still answers to the weightages: the KRA table's 100 points distribute the rated scores identically.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Self appraisal and Employee Performance Feedback
lessons.html:
Two structured inputs join the goal scores at the assessment window.

1. The self appraisal. On the Appraisal record, the employee completes the self-appraisal section by the published date:

1. The self ratings — the employee rates the KRAs (or the configured self-assessment rows) from their own view of the period.
2. The reflections — the free-text account: what was delivered, what blocked, what support is asked for. Instruct staff to write to the evidence — deliveries and dates — because the self appraisal is read beside the goal records and the feedback, and agreement between the three is what makes the final conversation short.

The self appraisal's weight in the final score is the configuration's setting (Chapter 6); its value is independent of its weight — the reflections are the employee's documented voice in their own assessment, and the outcome conversation (Chapter 7) starts from them.

2. The Employee Performance Feedback. Open Employee Performance Feedback (awesome bar) > New — or from the appraisal's feedback section. One record per reviewer per appraisal:

• The appraisal link and the reviewer — the manager per the reporting structure (module 1's Reports To), plus additional named reviewers where the policy uses them (a second reviewer for calibration, a cross-functional reviewer where the role serves another function).
• The rating rows — the template's Rating Criteria rendered as rating fields: every reviewer rates the same criteria (Chapter 2's structured-comparison design). Ratings follow the site's scale; anchor the scale in the policy (what a 3 means, what a 5 means) so two reviewers' numbers mean the same thing.
• The feedback text — the reviewer's account, written to observations: what was done, when, with what result. The recruitment module's rule restated: observations, not speculation.

3. Feedback discipline.

1. Feedback is submitted by the published date; the completion read (Chapter 7) lists the overdue by reviewer, and an assessment window that closes with missing feedback scores people on partial inputs — the read exists so it does not.
2. Each reviewer submits independently; calibration discussions happen at the calibration read (Chapter 7), on the submitted records, not before them.
3. Feedback is confidential per the policy's disclosure rule: the employee sees what the policy says they see, consistently for everyone. Decide the rule once, publish it with the cycle calendar, and configure access accordingly — the sensitive-data handling rules from module 1 apply to appraisal content throughout.

4. The period-long alternative. Where the site enables continuous feedback (feedback records created during the period, not only at the window), the same record and rules carry it; the assessment window then reads an accumulated file instead of a single retrospective. Use per the written policy; the mechanics do not change.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The final score
lessons.html:
The Appraisal record computes a final score from its inputs. This chapter covers the computation, its verification, and its handling.

1. The components. Per the cycle's configuration (Chapter 3, step 4), the final score combines:

1. The goal/KRA score — automated from goal progress, or manually rated, per the cycle's method (Chapter 4), weighted by the template's KRA weightages.
2. The self appraisal score — the employee's self ratings, at the configured share.
3. The feedback score — the reviewers' ratings averaged across the submitted Employee Performance Feedback records, at the configured share.

The shares are the policy's decision, published with the cycle calendar. The computation is visible on the appraisal: each component, its figure, its share, the total.

2. Verification, per appraisal, before scores are released.

1. Every component present: goals reviewed and confirmed (Chapter 4, step 4), self appraisal submitted, all named reviewers' feedback submitted. An appraisal scored on missing components is flagged, not released — the completeness rule.
2. The arithmetic spot-checked on a sample: components × shares = the final figure shown.
3. The template correct for the role (the Chapter 3 generation spot-check, re-run on any appraisal whose score is disputed).

3. What the score is and is not. Restating the Chapter 1 boundary as operating rules:

1. The score is a summary of recorded inputs — as good as the goals, ratings, and feedback behind it, and no better. The reads in Chapter 7 protect the inputs; nothing rescues a score built on stale goals and one reviewer's late guess.
2. The score informs decisions made elsewhere: the pay review reads it beside the movement record and the budget (the Payroll track, module 6); the promotion case reads it with the lifecycle documents (module 7). No lane in this module changes pay.
3. Score changes are governed: a disputed score is re-examined through its components — a goal's evidence, a rating's basis — and corrected through the records, never edited at the total. The appraisal's history (track changes per the standing audit rules) records any correction with its reason.

4. The outcome record. When the cycle's scores are final:

1. Each appraisal is submitted per document rules — the period's assessment closed as a record.
2. The outcome conversation (Chapter 7) is held and its summary noted on the appraisal: what was discussed, what was agreed, the training needs identified (module 6 reads these).
3. The cycle's decision pack (Chapter 7's distribution read plus the individual records) goes to the deciders for whatever the policy connects to the round — with every number traceable to its inputs.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The cycle reads and administration
lessons.html:
The reads that keep a cycle honest and complete, and the administration around them.

1. The completion read (weekly during the assessment window). From the cycle's appraisal list:

1. Self appraisals submitted versus total, overdue names listed.
2. Feedback submitted versus expected (appraisals × named reviewers), overdue by reviewer — the reviewer with eight overdue feedbacks is the bottleneck the read names while there is time to act.
3. Goals confirmed versus total (cycle start) and reviewed versus total (assessment window).

The read goes to HR's cycle owner and the responsible managers as a list; the cycle closes complete because the gaps were chased weekly, not discovered at the deadline.

2. The goal-freshness read (monthly during the period). Goals with no progress update in the month, by employee and manager — data to the managers per the standing rule. In automated cycles this read protects the scores directly; in manual cycles it protects the assessment's evidence.

3. The calibration read (before scores release). The draft score distribution by manager and by department:

1. A manager whose ratings sit far above or below the company distribution is a calibration conversation — about anchoring (what a 3 means), held on the records, before release.
2. The distribution itself is management data: presented as figures per the data-not-editorial rule; what the business does about its shape is the policy owner's decision.
3. Calibration adjusts ratings through their raters — a reviewer persuaded their anchoring was off revises their own feedback record with the change tracked. Nobody edits another's ratings.

4. The outcome conversation. Per appraisee, after scores are final: the manager and employee walk the record — goals, self appraisal, feedback, score — and agree the notes: outcomes, development actions, training needs. The conversation's summary is entered on the appraisal (Chapter 6, step 4). The training needs entered here are module 6's intake: a low-scored KRA with an agreed development action becomes a training-plan line.

5. Administration rules.

1. The cycle is scheduled, not improvised: the calendar published at start (Chapter 3), the reads on their cadence, the close on its date. An assessment round run by reminder-and-hope produces the missing-component scores Chapter 6 refuses.
2. Probation reviews are cycles: a probation confirmation runs as a small cycle (the probationers as appraisees, the probation template, the confirmation decision informed by the score) — the same machinery at smaller scale, and the confirmation date field (module 1) completed from its outcome.
3. Appraisal content is sensitive: access per the policy's disclosure rule, consistently; the permission matrix covers the appraisal doctypes; the confidentiality rules from the payroll track's slip handling apply in kind.
4. History stands: past cycles' appraisals are never revised to match later opinions; a correction has a cause and a tracked change; templates revise forward (Chapter 2).

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: the HealthTrade annual cycle
lessons.html:
This chapter applies Chapters 2-7 to HealthTrade. Configuration values and outcomes are listed per step.

Step 1 — templates (Chapter 2). Three Appraisal Templates built with the managers and confirmed by the MD:

• Branch Retail Staff — KRAs: Dispensing accuracy 35, Customer service 25, Stock control 25, Policy compliance 15. Criteria: Reliability, Communication, Compliance.
• Warehouse Operations — KRAs: Stock accuracy 35, Dispatch timeliness 30, Safety compliance 20, Housekeeping 15.
• Management — KRAs: Branch performance 40, Team development 25, Controls compliance 20, Reporting timeliness 15.

Weightage totals validate at 100; decision references recorded on each template.

Step 2 — the cycle (Chapter 3). Appraisal Cycle 2026 Annual created for the calendar year; thirty appraisees loaded by department filters and mapped to their templates. KRA evaluation method: manual rating for this first cycle — recorded on the cycle with the reason (goal discipline not yet established; the honest-records rule) and the intention to move to automated scoring next cycle once the goal rhythm holds. The final score shares confirmed and published with the cycle calendar: KRA rating 60, feedback 25, self appraisal 15.

Step 3 — goals anyway (Chapter 4). Goals are set at cycle start as working records even though this cycle scores manually: each appraisee drafts goals per KRA; managers confirm. Verification: every appraisee carries at least one confirmed goal per KRA. The monthly freshness read starts; month two lists nine stale goals across two branches — handed to the two managers as a list; month three lists two.

Step 4 — the assessment window (Chapters 5-6). The window opens on the calendar's date. The weekly completion read runs: week one — self appraisals 18/30, feedback 12/60 (two reviewers per appraisal: the manager and one second reviewer for calibration); week two — the read names one reviewer holding eight overdue feedbacks; the cycle owner escalates and the feedbacks arrive within the week; window close — 30/30 self appraisals, 60/60 feedbacks, all KRA ratings entered. Score verification: components complete on all thirty; the arithmetic sampled on five appraisals clean.

Step 5 — calibration and release (Chapter 7). The calibration read shows one branch's ratings averaging a full point above the company distribution; the anchoring conversation is held on the records, and the branch's second reviewer revises four of their own ratings with tracked changes and reasons. Scores release; outcome conversations run over two weeks; summaries and agreed actions entered on each appraisal.

Step 6 — the outputs. The decision pack to the MD: the distribution, the individual records. Seven training needs identified in the outcome notes (five on stock-control KRAs, two on reporting) — entered as module 6's training-plan intake. The pay review round that follows reads the scores beside the movement record per the Payroll track's procedure; every pay change that results travels that track's lanes. The cycle's close note records the method decision for next year: goal discipline held from month three, automated KRA scoring approved for the 2027 cycle.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common errors and the module rule
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in performance management, each with its correction and prevention.

Error 1 — templates without decisions. Symptom: equal-split weightages nobody chose; KRAs copied between unrelated roles; scores that answer to no stated priority. Correction: the KRAs and weightages redrafted with the role's manager and confirmed; the revision applied to the next cycle. Prevention: the template design procedure — manager drafts, owner confirms weightages, decision reference recorded.

Error 2 — automated scores over dead goals. Symptom: KRA scores computed from goals last updated at cycle start; assessment-week progress surges to 100%; scores nobody believes. Correction: the manager's evidence review before scores stand; unverifiable claims returned. Prevention: the honest method choice at cycle configuration and the monthly freshness read — automated scoring is adopted when the goal rhythm holds, not before.

Error 3 — the missing-component score. Symptom: finals computed with absent feedback or unsubmitted self appraisals; people scored on partial inputs. Correction: the missing components obtained and the score recomputed. Prevention: the weekly completion read with overdue names, and the completeness rule — flagged, not released.

Error 4 — uncalibrated raters. Symptom: one manager's team scoring systematically high or low; cross-team comparisons meaningless; the distribution driven by rater habits. Correction: the anchoring conversation on the records; raters revising their own ratings with tracked changes. Prevention: the scale anchored in the policy, and the calibration read before every release.

Error 5 — the score edited at the total. Symptom: final figures adjusted directly to match a desired outcome; components no longer explaining the total. Correction: the edit reversed; the disputed score re-examined through its components. Prevention: the rule that corrections travel through the records — a goal's evidence, a rating's basis — and the tracked history on the appraisal.

Error 6 — the appraisal executing pay. Symptom: pay changed on the appraisal conversation without the approval matrix, the letter, or the assignment; the payroll track's naked-assignment sweep catching the result. Correction: the change re-documented through the payroll lanes. Prevention: the Chapter 1 boundary operated — the score informs; the decision lanes execute.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: state the five record types and the pay boundary; build an Appraisal Template with weighted KRAs totalling 100 and rating criteria, through the design procedure; create an Appraisal Cycle with appraisee-template mapping, the evaluation method chosen honestly, and the published calendar; operate Goals — verifiable objectives per KRA, confirmed, fresh, evidence-reviewed; process self appraisals and Employee Performance Feedback with independent submission and the disclosure rule; verify and release final scores on complete components; and run the completion, freshness, and calibration reads with the outcome conversation.

Module rule 5: performance is assessed on records — templates weighted by decision, cycles run on a published calendar, scores computed from confirmed goals and submitted feedback, calibrated through the raters, and handed to the decision lanes as information, never as execution. Module 6 covers training and development.

training.title: HR 6 — Training & Development
training.desc: Training in ZhiftERP: the Training Program register with compliance flags; the Training Event — type, trainer, the employee table built from due populations, the invitation flow, and the required-training statement; Training Results entered within the week with absentee and retake lanes; Training Feedback to its two readers; the annual plan from the three intakes with owner approval, quarterly execution, and cost reconciliation; the four standing reads; and compliance training — the register, the expiry arithmetic on passing results, the renewal window, the lapse procedure, and the joiner and mover rules.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Training: scope and record structure
lessons.html:
This module covers training and development in ZhiftERP. On completing this module you will be able to: maintain Training Programs; create and run Training Events with their employee tables and status flow; record Training Results; collect Training Feedback; operate the training-needs intake and the annual training plan; and run the standing reads including the per-employee training record and the compliance-expiry read.

The record structure. Training uses four record types:

1. Training Program — the standing definition of a course or programme: what it covers, who delivers it (Chapter 2). One record per repeatable programme.
2. Training Event — one scheduled delivery: the date, location, trainer, and the employee table with invitation and attendance statuses (Chapter 3).
3. Training Result — the outcome record per employee per event: hours, grade, comments (Chapter 4).
4. Training Feedback — the attendee's assessment of the event (Chapter 4).

Where training needs come from. Three intakes feed the plan (Chapter 5):

1. The appraisal outcomes — module 5's outcome conversations produce agreed development actions per employee (the HealthTrade cycle produced seven); each is a plan line with a name attached.
2. The compliance calendar — trainings that regulation or policy requires on a cycle: the pharmacy regulatory refreshers, safety training, statutory inductions. These are obligations with expiry dates, tracked as such.
3. The business's own initiatives — new product lines, new procedures, system rollouts (the onboarding curriculum for new joiners is module 2's template; role-change training enters here).

Custody. HR administers the records and the plan; the content and its delivery belong to the trainers (internal or external); the compliance obligations belong to the compliance owner (the pharmacist superintendent for regulatory items, per the business's structure); attendance at required training is an instruction, not an invitation, and the policy says which trainings are which.

What reads training records.

1. The per-employee training record — the employee's event and result history (Chapter 6), read at appraisals, promotions, and audits.
2. The compliance-expiry read — who is current, who lapses when (Chapter 6), read monthly.
3. The plan-versus-delivered read — the year's plan against events held (Chapter 6), read quarterly and at the annual review.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the Training Program. Chapter 3: the Training Event. Chapter 4: Training Result and Training Feedback. Chapter 5: the needs intake and the annual plan. Chapter 6: the standing reads. Chapter 7: compliance training. Chapter 8: worked example. Chapter 9: review and the module rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Training Program
lessons.html:
Open Training Program (awesome bar) > New. One record per repeatable programme. Complete the fields in order.

1. Program Name. Name the programme for its content: Dispensing Standards Refresher, Stock Count Procedure, New Joiner Induction, Fire Safety.

2. Trainer details. The trainer's name, email, and contact — the internal deliverer (the senior pharmacist for dispensing standards; the operations lead for stock procedure) or the external provider's named contact. Where a programme alternates trainers, the programme record carries the default and each event (Chapter 3) carries its actual.

3. Description. The programme's content summary: the topics covered, the intended audience, the duration, and — for programmes with an assessment — what the result records (Chapter 4's grade basis). Write the description once here; every event created from the programme inherits the context, and the plan (Chapter 5) references programmes by these records.

4. Status. Active programmes are schedulable; retire superseded programmes by status rather than deletion (the standing never-delete rule — past events reference their programme, and the reference must stay readable).

The programme register. The Training Program list is the business's training catalogue. Maintain it deliberately:

1. One record per genuinely distinct programme — the same course delivered at two branches is one programme with two events, not two programmes.
2. Compliance programmes flagged as such in the description with their cycle stated (required annually for all dispensing staff) — Chapter 7 builds the expiry tracking on this.
3. The register reviewed annually with the training plan: programmes without an event in the year are confirmed still needed or retired; needs without a programme (the plan's new lines) get programme records before events are scheduled.

Sequencing note. Build the programme before its first event. An event created without a programme record works mechanically but leaves the catalogue incomplete: the per-employee training record (Chapter 6) groups by programme, the compliance read tracks by programme, and the plan plans by programme. The record costs two minutes; its absence costs every later read a gap.

Verification. Per programme: the name unambiguous, the trainer details current, the description stating audience and duration, compliance programmes carrying their cycle statement, status honest.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The Training Event
lessons.html:
Open Training Event (awesome bar) > New. One record per scheduled delivery. Complete the fields in order.

1. Event Name and Training Program. Name the event for its delivery — Dispensing Standards Refresher — Akure — March — and link the programme (Chapter 2).

2. Type. The delivery format from the type list: Seminar, Theory, Workshop, Conference, Exam, Internet, Self-Study. The type is a reporting dimension; select the honest format (a circulated self-study pack with a sign-off is Self-Study, and its result recording — Chapter 4 — is the sign-off).

3. Trainer Name and Trainer Email. The event's actual deliverer, pre-filled from the programme and adjusted where this delivery differs.

4. From Time, To Time, Location. The schedule and venue. For multi-session programmes, one event per session or one event spanning the block per the business's convention — decide once and record it, because the hours figure on results (Chapter 4) follows the convention.

5. Introduction. The attendee-facing note: what to prepare, what to bring, what the session covers. This text travels with the invitation.

6. The Employees table. The attendee list — one row per invited employee:

1. Add employees by the selection tools (department, branch, designation filters — the compliance read's due list in Chapter 7 is the standard source for refresher events).
2. Each row carries the employee and their status: Open on addition, then the invitation flow below.
3. For required trainings, the table is the coverage record: everyone due is on the list, and the gaps read (Chapter 6) compares the table against the due population.

7. Event Status. Scheduled → Completed (or Cancelled). The event is marked Completed when held; result recording (Chapter 4) follows completion.

The invitation flow.

1. With the event saved and the table built, send the invitations per the site's flow — attendee statuses move to Invited and the employees receive the event with the introduction text.
2. Confirmations per the site's self-service: attendees confirm and their status moves accordingly. For required trainings, the policy statement applies: attendance is an instruction; a non-confirmation is followed up by the manager, not left as a declined invitation.
3. On the day: attendance is recorded against the table (present rows progress; absentees stay visible as gaps). The attendance record here is the evidence the results and the compliance read stand on.

Scheduling procedure. Events are created from the plan (Chapter 5): the plan line names the programme, the audience, and the quarter; the event fixes the date, venue, and list. Publish the schedule ahead — branch staffing has to cover the absence, and the operations calendar (stock counts, peak days) is checked before dates are fixed, or the event competes with the work and loses.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Training Result and Training Feedback
lessons.html:
Two records close every event: the outcome per attendee and the attendee's assessment of the event.

1. The Training Result. Open Training Result (awesome bar) > New after the event completes — one result document per event, with a row per attendee:

• Employee — from the event's table; every attendee who was present gets a row. Absentees get no result row — their gap stays visible for the follow-up lane (below).
• Hours — the attended hours, per the event's convention (Chapter 3, step 4).
• Grade — where the programme assesses: the score or pass/fail per the programme's stated basis (Chapter 2's description). Where the programme does not assess, the grade records completion per the convention.
• Comments — the trainer's note per attendee where useful: observed gaps, recommended follow-up. Comments follow the standing observation rule — what was demonstrated, not speculation.

Submit the result document. The result rows are what the per-employee training record (Chapter 6) and the compliance read (Chapter 7) count — an event held but never resulted is invisible to both, and for this reason result entry is the event's closing step, dated within the week of delivery, not batched at quarter-end from memory.

2. The follow-up lane for absentees and failures.

1. Absentees from required training: rebooked onto the next event of the programme; the compliance read carries them as due until a result row exists. The manager is informed per the policy's required-training statement.
2. Failed assessments (where the programme's basis has a pass mark): the retake per the programme's rule, recorded as a new result row on the retake event; the compliance read treats an employee as current only on a passing result where the programme requires one.

3. The Training Feedback. Open Training Feedback (awesome bar) — one record per attendee per event, submitted through self-service after the event:

• The employee, the event, and the feedback text — the attendee's assessment of content, delivery, and usefulness.
• Collect feedback within the week (the same freshness rule as everywhere: assessment written later is reconstruction).

4. Reading the feedback. Per event, the feedback set goes to two readers:

1. The trainer — the delivery's own improvement input.
2. The plan owner — patterns across events: a programme whose feedback repeatedly names the same gap gets a content revision on the register; a venue or format that repeatedly fails gets a scheduling change. The read is quarterly with the plan read (Chapter 6), and it is data to its owners per the standing rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The needs intake and the annual plan
lessons.html:
The training plan turns needs into scheduled events. This chapter covers the intake, the plan document, and its operation.

1. The intake, from the three sources (Chapter 1).

1. Appraisal outcomes: after each cycle, HR extracts the agreed development actions from the outcome notes (module 5, Chapter 7) — each becomes an intake line: employee, need, source reference.
2. The compliance calendar: each compliance programme's cycle (Chapter 7) generates its due events for the year — audience and deadline fixed by the obligation.
3. Business initiatives: the owner's and managers' lines — new procedures, product knowledge, system training — entered with their sponsor named.

2. The plan document. One page per year, one line per planned training:

• The programme (from the register — needs without a programme get one first, Chapter 2), the audience (named employees or the population definition), the quarter, the sponsor/source (which intake line it serves), and the cost estimate where external.
• The plan is approved by the owner — training costs money and absence; the plan's approval is the budget's (the standing no-record-without-decision rule, applied to the year's training spend).
• Compliance lines are immovable by deadline; development and initiative lines schedule around the operations calendar.

3. Operating the plan through the year.

1. Each quarter's lines become Training Events (Chapter 3) at the quarter's start — dates fixed against the operations calendar, invitations out ahead.
2. The plan line closes when its event completes and results are recorded (Chapter 4's rule — an unresulted event closes nothing).
3. Mid-year additions (a new appraisal need, a regulatory change) enter as plan lines with their approval — the plan is a living document with a change record, not a January artefact.
4. The quarterly plan read (Chapter 6) tracks lines planned versus delivered versus resulted, and the year-end review closes the plan against outcomes.

4. Cost recording. External training costs post through the Accounts track's standard lanes (the Purchase Invoice against the provider, the expense account per the chart); the plan's cost column is reconciled against the posted costs at the quarterly read — the plan says what was approved; the ledger says what was spent; the two are read together.

5. The new-joiner tie. Induction training is a standing plan line executed through module 2's onboarding template (the orientation activity) plus the induction Training Event where the business runs a formal session — the joiner's first result rows begin their training record, and compliance programmes required from day one (the dispensing induction for pharmacy staff) are scheduled from the joining date per Chapter 7's cycle rules.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The standing reads
lessons.html:
Four reads keep training records useful. Each is stated with its source, cadence, and reader.

1. The per-employee training record. Source: the employee's Training Result rows across events, grouped by programme. Read on demand:

1. At appraisals — the period's training beside the goals and feedback (module 5's outcome conversation cites it: the development action agreed last cycle either has a result row or it does not).
2. At promotions and transfers (module 7) — the training history as part of the readiness evidence.
3. At audits — the regulator's or auditor's per-person question (show this pharmacist's regulatory training) answered from the rows: programme, event, date, hours, grade. The one-folder discipline from the payroll track applies in kind: the answer is a lookup, not an assembly.

2. The coverage/gaps read. Source: the event tables versus their due populations. Cadence: per required event, at scheduling and after delivery:

1. At scheduling: everyone due is on the table (Chapter 3's rule).
2. After delivery: attendees without result rows (absentees, failures) listed into the follow-up lane (Chapter 4) — the gap list is the rebooking list.

3. The plan read. Source: the plan document versus events and results. Cadence: quarterly, to the owner:

1. Lines planned versus events held versus results recorded, per quarter — slippage named while the year can still absorb it.
2. Cost approved versus cost posted (Chapter 5's reconciliation).
3. Feedback patterns per programme (Chapter 4's quarterly read) — the content and delivery notes beside the delivery figures.

4. The compliance-expiry read. Source: the compliance programmes' cycles against the latest passing result per employee. Cadence: monthly (Chapter 7 details the construction):

1. Current — employees whose latest passing result is inside the cycle.
2. Due — employees entering the renewal window (schedule them onto the next event).
3. Lapsed — employees past expiry: named to the compliance owner immediately, with the policy's consequence applied (a dispensing authorisation that lapses with the training is the compliance owner's call to make, on the read's data, the day the read shows it — not at the audit that finds it).

The reads' single rule. Every read above is a lookup over result rows. The reads are only as good as Chapter 4's discipline — results entered within the week of delivery, absentees left visible, retakes recorded. The register comparison habit from the payroll track applies: the read that runs monthly keeps the records honest weekly.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Compliance training
lessons.html:
Compliance trainings are obligations with cycles and consequences. This chapter is their specific machinery on the general records.

1. The compliance register. One page listing every training obligation:

• The programme (Chapter 2's record, flagged compliance with its cycle in the description), the obligation source (the regulation, the policy clause, the insurer's requirement), the population (who must hold it — by designation, by activity: all dispensing staff; all warehouse staff for safety induction), the cycle (annual, biennial, once-at-joining), and the owner (the compliance owner accountable for currency — the superintendent pharmacist for regulatory items, the operations lead for safety).

The register is confirmed with the compliance owner and reviewed annually — regulations change, and the register's review is where the change lands (a new obligation becomes a programme, a plan line, and a read, in that order).

2. The expiry computation. Per obligation, per employee in the population: the latest passing result row's date plus the cycle = the expiry. The monthly read (Chapter 6, read 4) buckets the population: current, due (inside the renewal window — set the window long enough to schedule an event: ninety days for annual cycles), lapsed.

3. The scheduling rule. Due lists drive events: the renewal event for a compliance programme is scheduled from the due bucket, inside the window, with the table built from the due names (Chapter 3, step 6). The compliance calendar's lines in the plan (Chapter 5) are placed at year start from the known expiries — compliance training is the most schedulable training there is, because the due dates are arithmetic.

4. The lapse procedure. A lapsed employee is named to the compliance owner the day the read shows it:

1. The owner applies the policy's consequence (the activity restriction where the obligation gates an activity — the decision is the owner's, on the record).
2. The remedial event is booked immediately; the result row restores currency.
3. The lapse is logged with its cause per the standing incident discipline — a lapse caused by the read not running is a process finding; a lapse caused by repeated non-attendance is a management matter, routed as data.

5. Joiners and movers.

1. Joiners: obligations required from day one enter the onboarding template (module 2) as activities; the first result rows are due within the policy's induction window, and the joiner appears in the population — and therefore the read — from their joining date.
2. Role changes (module 7's transfers and promotions): a move into a population (a stores assistant moving to dispensing) triggers the population's obligations from the move date; the transfer checklist carries the line.

6. The audit posture. Compliance training is audited by exactly the reads this module runs: the register (what obligations exist), the population definitions (who must hold what), the result rows (who holds what, with dates), and the expiry read (the currency picture). The payroll track's audit rules apply verbatim: answer from the records as kept, findings into the incident lane, never improve the past.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: HealthTrade training
lessons.html:
This chapter applies Chapters 2-7 to HealthTrade. Configuration values and outcomes are listed per step.

Step 1 — the programme register (Chapter 2). Six Training Programs created: Dispensing Standards Refresher (compliance — required annually for all dispensing staff; trainer: the superintendent pharmacist), Safety & Fire Induction (compliance — once at joining, refresher biennial; owner: operations lead), Stock Count Procedure, Cold Chain Handling (compliance — annual for warehouse and dispatch), New Joiner Induction, Reporting & Documentation Standards (created from the appraisal cycle's two reporting needs — module 5's intake).

Step 2 — the compliance register (Chapter 7). Three obligations listed with source, population, cycle, and owner: Dispensing Refresher (regulatory; eleven dispensing staff; annual; superintendent pharmacist), Safety Induction (policy/insurer; all thirty; once + biennial; operations lead), Cold Chain (policy; nine warehouse and dispatch staff; annual; operations lead). The expiry computation runs from existing records: seven of eleven dispensing staff have passing results inside the cycle; four are due within ninety days; none lapsed.

Step 3 — the annual plan (Chapter 5). The plan drafted from the three intakes: the compliance lines placed from the known expiries (the dispensing renewal event in Q1 for the four due, the full-population refresher in Q3; Cold Chain in Q2); the seven appraisal needs mapped (five stock-control needs → two Stock Count Procedure events at the branches; two reporting needs → the new Reporting Standards programme's first event); one initiative line (a supplier's product training, sponsor: the MD). Costs estimated on the external lines; the MD approves the plan.

Step 4 — an event end to end (Chapters 3-4). The Q1 dispensing renewal: Training Event created from the programme — type Workshop, the superintendent pharmacist as trainer, the Akure branch training room, the table built from the four due names plus two joiners inside their induction window. Invitations out three weeks ahead; the branch rota adjusted; all six confirm. The event completes; the Training Result document is entered the same week: six rows, hours four each, grades against the programme's pass basis — five pass, one fails the assessment. The retake books onto the Q3 event; the compliance read carries the one name as due-on-retake. Six Training Feedback records arrive within the week; one pattern noted (two attendees name the same module as rushed) for the trainer's next delivery.

Step 5 — the reads in rhythm (Chapter 6). Monthly compliance read: the due bucket empties after Q1 except the retake name; it restores at Q3. Quarterly plan read to the MD: Q1 — three lines delivered and resulted, one slipped to Q2 (venue clash with the stock count, caught at scheduling against the operations calendar the second time); costs posted match approvals. The per-employee record answers its first audit question in Q2 — the regulator's routine visit asks for two pharmacists' training evidence; the answer is two lookups: programme, event, date, hours, grade, on screen.

Result. Six programmes, a three-line compliance register with owners, an approved plan operating on the quarterly rhythm, events closing with same-week results and feedback, and the monthly expiry read keeping the compliance picture current — the audit answered from the records as kept.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common errors and the module rule
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in training administration, each with its correction and prevention.

Error 1 — events without results. Symptom: trainings held but invisible — no result rows; the per-employee record and the compliance read blind to delivered training. Correction: the results reconstructed from the event's attendance while evidence exists, noted as late-entered. Prevention: result entry as the event's closing step, dated within the week.

Error 2 — the catalogue of duplicates. Symptom: the same course as three programme records; per-employee histories fragmented; compliance tracking split across duplicates. Correction: the records merged to one programme per the master-data rules; events re-pointed. Prevention: one record per genuinely distinct programme, and the annual register review.

Error 3 — compliance by recollection. Symptom: no register, no cycles, no expiry read; currency asserted from memory; the lapse discovered by the audit or the incident. Correction: the register built with the compliance owner; the expiry computation run from existing results; lapses handled through the lapse procedure. Prevention: the register, the monthly read, and the ninety-day scheduling window.

Error 4 — the invitation treated as optional. Symptom: required trainings with voluntary-looking attendance; the same absentees every cycle; coverage gaps normalised. Correction: the policy's required-training statement applied — absentees rebooked and managers informed. Prevention: the statement published with the policy, the table-versus-population check at scheduling, and the follow-up lane after delivery.

Error 5 — the plan as a January artefact. Symptom: a plan written and abandoned; events improvised; appraisal needs never scheduled; the year-end review finding half the lines untouched. Correction: the plan re-baselined mid-year with its change record. Prevention: the quarterly plan read to the owner — planned versus delivered versus resulted, slippage named in time.

Error 6 — feedback collected and unread. Symptom: feedback records accumulating with no reader; the same delivery problems repeating across events. Correction: the backlog read once for patterns; the standing quarterly read instituted. Prevention: the two named readers — the trainer per event, the plan owner per quarter.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: state the four record types and the three needs intakes; maintain the programme register with compliance flags and the annual review; run a Training Event — the employee table from the due population, the invitation flow, the required-training statement, attendance on the day; record Training Results within the week with the absentee and retake lanes, and collect Training Feedback to its two readers; operate the annual plan — intake, approval, quarterly execution, cost reconciliation; run the four standing reads; and operate compliance training — the register, the expiry computation, the scheduling window, the lapse procedure, and the joiner and mover rules.

Module rule 6: training is delivered as records — programmes catalogued once, events run from the plan with full tables, results entered within the week, compliance tracked by arithmetic on passing results, and every question answered from the rows as kept. Module 7 covers lifecycle events and separation.
