lifecycle.title: HR 7 — Lifecycle Events & Separation
lifecycle.desc: Lifecycle events in ZhiftERP: the Employee Transfer with its property table, honest dates, and cross-track lines; the Employee Promotion with the silent-difference check and the pay boundary; the Employee Grievance entered as stated, routed per policy, investigated as observations, and resolved on the record; the Employee Separation generated from its template beside the payroll exit, with the Exit Interview on its rules; probation confirmations and contract renewals decided on time from the monthly reads; and the movement record with its quarterly both-ways reconciliation.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Lifecycle events: scope and record structure
lessons.html:
This module covers the employment lifecycle events between joining and exit in ZhiftERP. On completing this module you will be able to: execute transfers through the Employee Transfer document; execute promotions through the Employee Promotion document with the pay boundary operated; record and resolve grievances through the Employee Grievance document; run separations through the Employee Separation document and its template; conduct the Exit Interview; and operate probation confirmations and contract renewals on their standing reads.

The record structure. Lifecycle events use five record types:

1. Employee Transfer — the document that moves an employee between branches, departments, or companies, applying the property changes from its date (Chapter 2).
2. Employee Promotion — the document that changes designation and related properties from its date (Chapter 3).
3. Employee Grievance — the record of a raised grievance, its investigation, and its resolution (Chapter 4).
4. Employee Separation — the exit's task checklist, generated from a template like onboarding (Chapter 5).
5. Exit Interview — the structured exit conversation's record (Chapter 5).

The design principle, carried from module 1. Every lifecycle event is a change to the Employee master executed as a document: the document carries the decision, the date, and the property changes; the master's history shows what changed, when, and on whose authority. The alternative — editing Employee fields directly when someone moves — leaves the same fields changed with no document stating why, and the standing rule applies: no change without its record.

The boundaries with other tracks, stated once.

1. Pay: a transfer or promotion that changes pay executes the pay change through the Payroll track's lanes (the approval matrix, the letter, the Salary Structure Assignment — its module 6). The lifecycle document applies the organisational properties; it does not carry the pay change.
2. The exit: the Payroll track's module 7 owns the exit's money — the final slip, encashment, the settlement, the release checklist. This module owns the exit's HR side — the separation checklist, the exit interview, the record closure — and the two run together: the separation template's activities include the payroll lines, and both meet at the two-field rule (Relieving Date, Status).
3. Access: the sysadmin's joiner/mover/leaver procedures execute the access side of every event here; the checklists carry the confirmation lines.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the Employee Transfer. Chapter 3: the Employee Promotion. Chapter 4: the Employee Grievance. Chapter 5: the Employee Separation and the Exit Interview. Chapter 6: probation confirmations and contract renewals. Chapter 7: the lifecycle reads. Chapter 8: worked example. Chapter 9: review and the module rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Employee Transfer
lessons.html:
Open Employee Transfer (awesome bar) > New. One document per move. Complete the fields in order.

1. Employee. Select the employee being transferred.

2. Transfer Date. The effective date, from the documented decision (the transfer memo, the approved request). The properties apply from this date; the date is the decision's, entered exactly — the honest-date rule from the payroll track applies to organisational changes identically.

3. The transfer details table. One row per Employee property the transfer changes:

• Property — the field being changed: Branch, Department, Designation (where the move changes role), Reports To, Holiday List (where the destination's working pattern differs), Payroll Cost Center (where cost addressing is per employee — the branch move that forgets this row posts the salary to the old branch's P&L from the transfer date).
• Current — pre-filled from the record.
• New — the destination value, from its master.

Build the row set from a standing transfer checklist of properties, not from memory — the table's completeness is the transfer's quality: each property forgotten is a report, a routing, or a posting that stays wrong until someone notices.

4. Inter-company transfers. Where the move crosses legal entities, the transfer handles the company change per the site's configuration (including the new-employee-record option where the destination company requires its own record — the Payroll track, module 8's rule: employment is per company). An inter-company move is an exit-and-join in legal substance: the payroll and statutory consequences run with the accountant (final computations in the origin company per its rules, fresh assignment in the destination), and the transfer document coordinates the organisational side.

5. Submit. On submission the property changes apply to the Employee record from the transfer date. Verify after submission: the Employee record's changed fields, the Organizational Chart where Reports To moved, and the destination's approver routing picking the employee up (module 1, Chapter 7's designs).

The transfer procedure.

1. The decision documented and approved per the business's design; attached to the transfer.
2. The property rows built from the checklist; the pay question answered explicitly — pay changes, if any, routed to the payroll lanes with the transfer referenced.
3. The document submitted effective the honest date.
4. The cross-track lines confirmed: access changes per the sysadmin mover procedure (role/branch scoping); compliance obligations triggered by the destination population (module 6, Chapter 7 — the stores-to-dispensing move's training line); the destination Holiday List and shift arrangements (module 3) in place before the first working day.
5. The verification reads run (step 5 above) and the transfer noted on the movement record (Chapter 7).

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The Employee Promotion
lessons.html:
Open Employee Promotion (awesome bar) > New. One document per promotion. The Payroll track's module 6 covered this document from the pay side; this chapter is the HR execution.

1. Employee and Promotion Date. The employee and the effective date from the approved decision — the promotion letter is the anchor document (the payroll track's letter rule), and the date here is the letter's date.

2. The promotion details table. One row per property the promotion changes:

• Designation — the new title, from the Designation master (the promotion's defining row).
• Grade — where grades are in use, the new grade (and the payroll consequence of a grade's Default Salary Structure is verified against the letter at the assignment — never assumed from the default).
• Department / Reports To — where the promotion changes the reporting position (the new supervisor's own reports re-pointed per module 1, Chapter 7 where the promotion creates a manager).

3. The silent-difference check. The payroll track's finding, restated as the HR-side procedure: when the promotion moves the employee between salary structures (a different package family), the two structures' component lists are compared line by line before the letter finalises — a component present in one and absent in the other (the meal allowance absent from the Management structure) is a difference the letter must state, or payday delivers it as a surprise. The comparison is the promotion checklist's line, run with the payroll operator.

4. Submit. The property changes apply from the promotion date. The pay change — where the promotion carries one — travels the payroll lanes in full: the approval on the matrix, the letter, the Salary Structure Assignment from the same effective date. The promotion document and the assignment reference each other; the payroll track's quarterly naked-assignment sweep verifies the pairing from its side, and the movement record (Chapter 7) carries the event from this side.

The promotion procedure.

1. The case assembled: the appraisal history (module 5's records — the readiness evidence), the role's requirements (the Designation description), the training record (module 6).
2. The decision approved per the matrix; the letter issued stating title, effective date, pay terms, and any structure differences (step 3's check).
3. The Employee Promotion document entered and submitted effective the letter's date; the assignment entered by the payroll operator from the same letter.
4. The cross-track lines: access changes where the new role carries them (the sysadmin mover procedure — the new manager's approver roles); approver-table updates where the promotion makes the employee an approver (module 1's department tables); compliance obligations of the new population where any.
5. Verification: the Employee record's properties, the Organizational Chart, the first slip after the effective date read against the letter (the payroll operator's line, confirmed jointly).

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The Employee Grievance
lessons.html:
Open Employee Grievance (awesome bar) > New. One record per raised grievance. The record's discipline is the chapter's substance: grievances handled off the record produce disputes with no facts.

1. The record's fields.

• Raised By / Subject — the employee raising it and the grievance's subject line.
• Grievance Type — from the type master (create the categories per the written grievance policy: working conditions, conduct, pay dispute, harassment, other). The type routes and reports; a harassment type in particular carries the policy's specific handling requirements.
• Grievance Against — the party the grievance concerns, per the form's structure.
• Date, Description, and Cause — the account as raised, entered as stated: the record holds the raiser's account in the raiser's terms, and the investigation's findings are entered separately (below), not blended into the original account.
• Status — Open → Investigated → Resolved (or Invalid per the policy's finding).
• Resolution fields — the resolution detail, the resolved-by, and the date.

2. The handling procedure, per the written grievance policy.

1. Receipt: the grievance entered on the day it is raised (by the employee through self-service where enabled, or by HR on the employee's behalf with the authority noted — the no-proxy rule from module 4 applies in kind). The raiser receives the acknowledgment the policy promises, with the timeline.
2. Routing: per type and per the policy — the line manager for working-conditions matters, HR and the owner for conduct matters, the policy's named route for harassment (which never routes through the person complained about — the routing design is checked for this before the first grievance, not during it).
3. Investigation: the investigator gathers the facts and enters findings in the resolution section as observations with their sources — the recruitment module's rule (observations, not speculation) applies with full weight here. Pay-dispute grievances route through the payroll query procedure (its module 4) for the arithmetic and return here for any policy matter the arithmetic exposes.
4. Resolution: the decision per the policy's authority, entered with its reasoning; the status moved; the raiser informed per the policy's communication line.
5. Confidentiality: grievance records are among the most sensitive records in the system — the access matrix restricts them to the handling roles, and the module 1 sensitive-data rules apply at their strictest.

3. The grievance reads. Quarterly, to the owner, as figures: grievances by type, by status age (an Open grievance aging past the policy's timeline is a process failure regardless of its merits), and by unit. The read is data per the standing rule — a unit's grievance cluster is the owner's signal to look, and the records give the look its facts.

4. What the record protects. Both parties. The raiser has a dated record that the matter was raised and what was done; the business has a dated record of its handling; the person complained about has findings entered as observations rather than accumulated impressions. The employment disputes that reach lawyers are argued from exactly these records — or from their absence.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The Employee Separation and the Exit Interview
lessons.html:
The exit's HR machinery: the separation checklist and the structured exit conversation. The Payroll track's module 7 runs the money; this chapter runs beside it.

1. The Employee Separation Template. Open Employee Separation Template (awesome bar) > New — built once, like the onboarding template (module 2, Chapter 7), with one row per exit activity:

• The activity, the responsible user or role, and the timing relative to the relieving date.
• Standard rows: the two-field entry — Relieving Date and Status — on the decision's day (HR); the leave balance confirmation with the employee at the exit's start (HR — the payroll track's encashment reads it); the handover of duties documented (the manager); the direct reports re-pointed where the leaver manages (HR, module 1's rule); the exit interview scheduled and held (HR — below); company property collected against the custody list (Administration); access closure on the relieving date (the sysadmin's leaver procedure — confirmed, not assumed); the payroll settlement lines (the payroll operator — the settlement sheet, the statutory tail, the release checklist per that track); the record closure — Reason for Leaving, exit fields, attachments complete (HR).

2. The Employee Separation document. Open Employee Separation > New at exit confirmation: the employee, the relieving date, the template. Submission generates the activity tasks to their owners with dates — the exit as a visible checklist across four functions instead of a corridor coordination. The boarding status tracks completion; the exit closes when every activity does, and the payroll track's release checklist and this document confirm each other's lines at the end.

3. The Exit Interview. Open Exit Interview (awesome bar) > New — the structured exit conversation's record:

• The employee (the relieving date and details pulled from the record), the interviewer (per the policy — HR or a manager not in the leaver's line, so the conversation can be candid), the scheduled date, and the status.
• The interview runs on the policy's standing question set — the reasons for leaving in the leaver's terms, the experience of the role and management, what the business should know — and the responses are recorded as given (the as-stated rule from Chapter 4).
• Held before the last day where possible (the last-afternoon interview competes with goodbyes and loses), and never made a condition of the settlement — the payroll track's release checklist does not include it, deliberately: the interview is the business asking a favour of someone leaving, and its honesty depends on that being true.

4. Reading the exits. Two instruments, quarterly and annually:

1. The attrition read — leavers by Reason for Leaving (module 1's field), by unit, by tenure band: the turnover picture as figures. A unit whose leavers cluster in the first year is an onboarding or management signal; a reason category rising across units is a policy signal. Data to the owner per the standing rule.
2. The exit-interview themes — the interviews read together for recurring themes, summarised without attribution per the policy's confidentiality line. The themes join the attrition figures in the annual review: the numbers say who leaves; the interviews say why in their own words; the two together are the retention conversation's facts.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Probation confirmations and contract renewals
lessons.html:
Two scheduled lifecycle events that fail silently when untracked. Both run on standing reads from module 1's fields.

1. Probation confirmations.

1. The read: monthly, the Employee list filtered on probation-period fields — probation end dates falling in the next sixty days, by manager. The list goes to the managers with the confirmation procedure attached.
2. The assessment: the probation review runs as a small appraisal cycle (module 5, Chapter 7's rule): the probation template, the manager's assessment on the record, the decision informed by the score.
3. The outcomes, each as a record: confirmed — the confirmation letter issued, the confirmation date field completed on the Employee record, any terms that change at confirmation (the policy's probation terms) executed through their lanes; extended — where the policy allows extension: the letter stating the extension and its reasons, the field updated, the next review scheduled; not confirmed — the exit per the probation terms, through the full separation machinery (Chapter 5 and the payroll track's module 7 — a probation exit is an exit, with every checklist line).
4. The failure mode named: the probation that lapses into confirmation by silence — the end date passing with no assessment, the employee confirmed by default with no record. The monthly read exists to make the silent lapse impossible: every end date gets a decision, dated, on the record.

2. Contract renewals.

1. The read: monthly, the expiring-contracts report (module 1, Chapter 3's contract end date field) — contracts ending in the next ninety days, by unit. Ninety days because the decision needs time on both sides: the business deciding, the employee planning.
2. The decision, each as a record: renewed — the new contract signed before the old expires; the contract end date updated from the new document; the terms changes, if any, through their lanes; converted — the fixed-term becoming permanent per the decision: the letter, the Employment Type updated (module 1's master), the policy consequences (leave policy differences by type — module 4) executed from the conversion date; ended — the contract expiring per its terms: the exit through the separation machinery, scheduled from the known date (the most schedulable exit there is — the payroll track's retirement observation applies: known dates make clean exits).
3. The failure mode named: the contract that expires unnoticed — the employee working on, the legal position unclear, the eventual regularisation done backwards. The blank end date on a fixed-term record (module 1's warning) and the skipped monthly read are the two causes; the register hygiene filter and the standing read are the two preventions.

3. The shared pattern. Both events are date arithmetic on maintained fields plus a decision lane. The pattern repeats across the programme — the compliance expiries (module 6), the payroll year lines, the holiday list build — and it is the module's demonstration case for Chapter 9's rule: scheduled events are read from the records on a calendar, decided on time, and executed as documents.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The lifecycle reads and the movement record
lessons.html:
The standing instruments across all lifecycle events.

1. The movement record. The payroll track (module 6) keeps the movement record for pay events; the HR side extends it to all lifecycle events — one register, one line per event:

• The employee, the event type (transfer, promotion, confirmation, extension, renewal, conversion, separation), the effective date, the document reference, and the decision reference.
• Maintained as events execute (the procedure chapters each end by noting the event here), and read quarterly against the documents: every line has its document; every lifecycle document has its line. The reconciliation is the same both-ways read as everywhere else in the programme.

2. The quarterly lifecycle read, to the owner. One page of figures:

1. Events by type for the quarter (the movement record's counts).
2. The attrition figures (Chapter 5's read).
3. The scheduled-event health: probation decisions made versus due; contract decisions made versus due; any lapse listed with its cause (Chapter 6's failure modes, counted).
4. Open grievances by age against the policy timeline (Chapter 4).

3. The cross-track confirmations, gathered. Every lifecycle event touches other tracks, and each procedure chapter carried confirmation lines. Gathered here as the standing checklist rows any event's document should show completed:

1. Access — the sysadmin's joiner/mover/leaver procedure line, confirmed on the event's checklist (the transfer's scoping change, the promotion's new roles, the separation's same-day closure).
2. Pay — where the event carries a pay consequence: the payroll lanes' documents referenced from the lifecycle document (the assignment, the letter).
3. Compliance — population changes triggering training obligations (module 6's mover rule).
4. Routing — approver tables and Reports To updated where the event changes them (module 1).

4. The history discipline, restated for lifecycle. Lifecycle documents apply changes forward from honest dates; the Employee record's history (track changes per the standing audit configuration) shows the sequence. Three rules:

1. Backdating is the honest-date lane only: an event executed late is entered with its true effective date and processed with its true entry date — the arrears pattern from the payroll track, applied to organisational changes (the transfer applied a month late corrects reports and routing forward, and the gap is noted, not hidden).
2. Documents are never cancelled to rewrite outcomes: a wrong transfer is corrected by a correcting transfer with its cause noted.
3. The Employee record's Version history plus the movement record together answer any question of the form when did this person's role change and on whose authority — the answer is two lookups, which is the standard the whole module builds to.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: a HealthTrade quarter of lifecycle events
lessons.html:
This chapter applies Chapters 2-7 to one HealthTrade quarter. Configuration values and outcomes are listed per event.

Event 1 — a transfer (Chapter 2). A warehouse assistant moves from Central Lagos to the Akure branch on the operations manager's approved memo. Employee Transfer entered: transfer date the 1st; property rows — Branch (Central Lagos → Akure), Department (unchanged), Reports To (the Akure branch manager), Holiday List (Standard → Retail Branches — Akure works Saturdays), Payroll Cost Center (Central Lagos → Akure). Submitted; verification: the record's fields, the chart, and the first post-transfer slip's cost center confirmed with the payroll operator. The compliance line fires: Akure's role includes dispatch handling — the Cold Chain obligation triggers from the move date and the employee joins the Q2 event's table (module 6's mover rule executed). Movement record: one line, memo referenced.

Event 2 — a promotion (Chapter 3). A senior pharmacy technician is promoted to Pharmacy Counter supervisor. The case: two appraisal cycles' records, the training record showing the supervision programme completed. The silent-difference check runs with the payroll operator: the destination structure carries a Responsibility Allowance absent from the origin — stated in the letter. Employee Promotion entered effective the letter's date: Designation and Reports To rows; the counter staff re-pointed to the new supervisor; the department approver table updated (the new supervisor joins the leave approvers). The assignment enters from the same letter; the first slip is read jointly against it. Movement record: one line, letter referenced.

Event 3 — a grievance (Chapter 4). A driver raises a working-conditions grievance (vehicle safety) through self-service. Entered as stated, type Working Conditions, routed to the operations manager per the policy. Investigation findings entered as observations: two of the raised items verified (a worn tyre set, a faulty jack), one not reproduced. Resolution: the verified items fixed with dates, the resolution recorded, the raiser informed; status Resolved in eleven days against the policy's fourteen-day timeline. The quarterly read carries it as one line.

Event 4 — a separation (Chapter 5). An accounts assistant resigns with notice (the payroll track's module 7 worked example is this exit's money side; this is the HR side). Employee Separation generated from the template: nine activities across HR, the manager, Administration, the sysadmin, and the payroll operator. The Exit Interview is held four days before the last day by the HR lead (not the line manager); responses recorded as given. All activities close by the relieving date; the separation's checklist and the payroll release checklist confirm each other's lines. The attrition read gains one line: resignation, Finance, tenure three years.

Event 5 — the scheduled reads (Chapter 6). The monthly probation read lists one name — assessed as a small cycle, confirmed, the letter issued and the confirmation date field completed. The contract read lists two contracts ending inside ninety days: one renewed (new contract signed three weeks before expiry, end date updated), one converted to permanent (Employment Type updated, the leave policy difference executed from the conversion date per module 4).

The quarter's close. The movement record shows seven lines, each with its document; the both-ways reconciliation is clean. The quarterly page to the MD: seven events by type, one resignation, probation and contract decisions two-for-two on time, zero lapses, one grievance resolved inside the timeline. Every figure traces to a document in two lookups.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common errors and the module rule
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in lifecycle administration, each with its correction and prevention.

Error 1 — the fields edited instead of the document. Symptom: Branch, Designation, or Reports To changed directly on the Employee record; the change real but undocumented; the movement record silent. Correction: the event documented retrospectively — the lifecycle document entered with the honest dates and the late entry noted. Prevention: the rule that lifecycle changes travel through their documents, and the quarterly both-ways reconciliation catching direct edits.

Error 2 — the incomplete property table. Symptom: the transfer that moved the branch but not the cost center, the holiday list, or the reporting line; the salary posting to the old branch, the leave counting the wrong calendar. Correction: the missing rows applied by a correcting document. Prevention: the standing property checklist at transfer entry — the table built from the list, not from memory.

Error 3 — the promotion pay surprise. Symptom: the promoted employee's first slip differing from expectation; a component present in one structure and absent in the other, discovered on payday. Correction: the payroll query procedure, then the letter or structure corrected per the decision. Prevention: the silent-difference check — the two structures compared line by line with the payroll operator before the letter finalises.

Error 4 — the grievance off the record. Symptom: complaints handled in conversations; no dated record of what was raised or done; the eventual dispute argued from recollections. Correction: the matter entered when it resurfaces, with its history as reconstructable. Prevention: the entry-on-the-day rule, the routing design checked in advance, and the quarterly age read.

Error 5 — the silent lapse. Symptom: probations confirmed by default; contracts expired with the employee working on; the regularisation done backwards under pressure. Correction: the position regularised through the proper documents with honest dates and the gap noted. Prevention: the monthly probation and contract reads — date arithmetic on maintained fields, decided on time.

Error 6 — the separation as one person's memory. Symptom: exits coordinated by corridor; the property unreturned, the access alive, the interview skipped, the reports orphaned — each discovered later. Correction: the open items closed through their owners. Prevention: the Employee Separation template — the exit as generated tasks with owners and dates, confirmed against the payroll release checklist.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: state the five lifecycle record types and the three track boundaries; execute a transfer with the complete property table and the cross-track lines; execute a promotion with the silent-difference check and the pay boundary; record, route, investigate, and resolve a grievance per the written policy with the as-stated and observations rules; run a separation from the template with the Exit Interview held on its rules; operate the probation and contract reads with every outcome as a record; and maintain the movement record with the quarterly reconciliation and owner's page.

Module rule 7: lifecycle events are documents — transfers and promotions applying their property rows from honest dates, grievances entered as stated and resolved on the record, separations run as generated checklists beside the payroll exit, and every scheduled event decided on time from the standing reads. Module 8 closes the track: settings, the assembled controls, and the handover test.

advanced_hr.title: HR 8 — Advanced HR: Settings, Analytics & Structure
advanced_hr.desc: The structural close of the HR track: the HR Settings walk — naming, retirement age, approval and backdating flags, vacancy checking, mobile checkin — recorded with reasons; the control register assembling the track's reads with owners, cadences, and evidence locations; the HR calendar from daily reads to the annual block scheduled before its season; the standing reports built to the two-lookup traceability standard; data protection by access matrix and retention convention; multi-company HR on the legal separation; the handover and absence tests; and the track's eight rules.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The structural close of the HR track
lessons.html:
The final module assembles the HR function. On completing this module you will be able to: walk the HR Settings page and record its decisions; assemble the track's controls into one register with the HR calendar; run the standing HR reports as management data; operate the data-protection rules across the HR doctypes; run the handover and absence tests for the HR function; and state the track's eight rules.

Where the track stands. Modules 1-7 built the machinery: the Employee master and its hygiene, the recruitment pipeline, attendance, leave, performance, training, and the lifecycle documents. Each module left artifacts — registers, procedures, reads, checklists. This module's work is structure: the same close the other tracks ran — making the collection into a function that runs the same regardless of who runs it.

The three structural claims.

1. The settings are written decisions (Chapter 2): the HR Settings page walked field by field, each value carrying its owner, date, and reason — the payroll track's settings rule applied to the HR configuration.
2. The controls are one system (Chapters 3-4): the modules' reads and registers gathered onto one control page with one calendar, visible to the operator, the owner, and the auditor.
3. The function survives its operator (Chapters 5-7): the data handled lawfully and consistently, the reports answering from records, and the handover test passed — the programme's standing final test.

Custody, closed where it opened. HR operates the machinery and keeps its evidence; the policies — employment terms, leave, performance, grievance, training — are the business's written decisions; the owner decides; the other functions (payroll, sysadmin, accounts) meet HR at the documented boundaries every module stated. The operator's standing rule holds to the last page: the records state what the decisions stated, and every figure traces to its document.

How this module is used. Chapters 2-4 are built once and then operated: the settings walk and the register in one working session each, the calendar published at year start. Chapters 5-7 are standing disciplines: the reports on their cadence, the data rules continuously, the absence test on its schedule. Chapter 8 shows the whole set running for one business year; Chapter 9 closes the track.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the HR Settings walk. Chapter 3: the control register. Chapter 4: the HR calendar. Chapter 5: the reports and data protection. Chapter 6: multi-company HR. Chapter 7: the handover test. Chapter 8: worked example. Chapter 9: the eight rules.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The HR Settings walk
lessons.html:
Open HR Settings (awesome bar). Walk every field, decide each with its owner, and record the decision on the settings page — value, owner, date, one-line reason. The walk is the routine change occasion; between walks the page is stable.

1. The employee block.

1. Employee Naming By — naming series, employee number, or full name. The naming-series decision (module 1, Chapter 3) is confirmed here; changing it mid-register renames nothing retroactively and confuses everything, so the value is set at implementation and left.
2. Retirement Age — feeds the retirement-date computation from Date of Birth (module 1). Set from the written employment policy; the annual read of approaching retirement dates joins the calendar (Chapter 4) — the retirement is the payroll track's best-case exit precisely because this field makes its date known years ahead.
3. Standard Working Hours — where the site uses a standard-hours figure in computations, set from the policy and recorded with what reads it.

2. The leave and expense approval block.

4. Leave Approver Mandatory / Expense Approver Mandatory — whether applications require a named approver to submit. Set per the routing design (module 1, Chapter 7): with department-table routing maintained, mandatory flags enforce that no application floats unrouted.
5. Restrict Backdated Leave Application (and the role permitted where restricted) — whether ordinary users can enter leave for past dates. The recommended posture: restricted, with the permitted role held by HR — backdated leave is the honest-date lane's controlled exception (the sickness applied for on return — module 4), entered by the role that documents it, and the restriction is what keeps the exception a lane instead of a habit.
6. The leave notification settings — the application and approval notifications per the site's options: on, so the workflow moves without chasing, with the templates checked once for tone and content.

3. The hiring block.

7. Check Vacancies — whether Job Openings validate against the Staffing Plan (module 2, Chapter 2's control). On where plans are in use — this switch is the plan-first order's enforcement.
8. The interview reminder settings — interview and feedback reminders per the options: on, with the same-day feedback rule (module 2, Chapter 5) stated in the reminder text where the template allows.

4. The attendance block.

9. Allow Employee Checkin from Mobile App (and the location-capture option where present) — per the business's field-staff policy (module 3, Chapter 3's mobile source). Where enabled, the policy states who may use it and the location-capture posture is communicated to staff before it is switched on — a tracking capability enabled silently is a grievance generator; the same capability stated in policy is a working tool.

5. The record. The settings page's record carries every field above with its four columns. Fifteen minutes at the walk; re-walked annually with the control register (Chapter 3); changed between walks only through the standing change discipline with the record updated.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The HR control register
lessons.html:
The track's controls, gathered from their modules onto one page — every control with its owner, cadence, and evidence location. Three readers use it: the operator as the working map, the owner for oversight sampling, the auditor as the visit's starting point.

The register's rows, by module.

Module 1 — the Employee register: the joiner verification per new record (HR, per event, the verification comment); the monthly blank-field filters — Reports To, Holiday List, Preferred Contact Email, Payroll Cost Center — target zero (HR, monthly, the filter results); the quarterly approver sweep and attachment sample (HR, quarterly, the sweep note).

Module 2 — recruitment: the plan-first order with Check Vacancies on (system-enforced, continuous); the weekly funnel and aging reads during active hiring (HR, weekly, the read list); the offer-equals-assignment check at joining (HR + payroll, per hire, the verification comment).

Module 3 — attendance: the daily sync-and-count read per device location (HR/sysadmin, daily, the day note); the weekly sheet gap read (HR, weekly, the closed gaps); the records-close completeness line (HR, monthly, the payroll checklist's line 4); the monthly pattern and request-lane reads (HR, monthly, the summaries).

Module 4 — leave: the annual entitlement round with the completeness verification (HR, annual, allocations = employees × rows); the monthly close read — no Open applications on the closed month, the LWP list to payroll (HR, monthly, the list); the quarterly ledger reconciliation sample (HR, quarterly, the sample note).

Module 5 — performance: the weekly completion read in windows (HR, per cycle, the overdue lists); the monthly goal-freshness read (HR, monthly in-period, the stale list); the calibration read before release (HR + owner, per cycle, the distribution page).

Module 6 — training: results-within-the-week per event (HR, per event, the result document's date); the monthly compliance-expiry read (HR + compliance owner, monthly, the bucket list); the quarterly plan read (HR to owner, quarterly, the plan page).

Module 7 — lifecycle: the monthly probation and contract reads (HR, monthly, the decision records); the quarterly movement-record reconciliation (HR, quarterly, the both-ways note); the quarterly grievance age read (HR to owner, quarterly, the age list).

The register's operation.

1. The page is reviewed annually with the settings walk: controls confirmed, owners current, evidence locations true. A control that found nothing all year is assessed by the standing question — redundant or working — and the payroll track's answer usually holds: the control that finds nothing is usually preventing what it would find.
2. The owner samples unannounced: any row, its evidence produced in one lookup. The sample failing — evidence that needs assembly — is itself the finding.
3. Every control's output that is management data (patterns, distributions, ages) goes to its named reader per the data-not-editorial rule, on the register's cadence.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The HR calendar
lessons.html:
The function's scheduled lines, gathered from the modules into one calendar. Each line carries its owner and its module reference; the calendar is published at year start and reviewed with the register.

Daily.

1. The attendance sync-and-count read per device location (module 3).
2. New grievances entered on the day raised (module 7).

Weekly.

3. The attendance sheet gap read per location (module 3).
4. During active hiring: the funnel and aging reads (module 2).
5. During assessment windows: the completion read (module 5).

Monthly.

6. The Employee register blank-field filters (module 1).
7. The records-close block, aligned to the payroll close date: attendance complete, leave decided, the LWP list handed over (modules 3-4 — the two tracks' standing meeting point).
8. The compliance-expiry read (module 6).
9. The probation and contract reads — sixty and ninety days ahead respectively (module 7).
10. The joiners and leavers lists to the payroll reconciliation (module 1).
11. In-period: the goal-freshness read (module 5).

Quarterly.

12. The approver sweep and attachment sample (module 1).
13. The leave ledger reconciliation sample (module 4).
14. The training plan read to the owner; the feedback pattern read (module 6).
15. The movement-record reconciliation and the lifecycle page to the owner (module 7).
16. The grievance age read (module 7).
17. The source-effectiveness read where hiring ran (module 2).

Annually.

18. The Holiday List build for the new year, with the per-employee assignment sweep (module 3 — scheduled in the last quarter).
19. The leave entitlement round: the new Leave Period, the policy confirmation, the Policy Assignments, carry-forward, the completeness verification (module 4 — December, before the year turns).
20. The appraisal cycle per the performance policy's calendar (module 5).
21. The training plan drafted from the three intakes and approved (module 6 — with the compliance lines placed from known expiries).
22. The programme and compliance register reviews (module 6); the type register re-read (module 4); the template reviews (module 5).
23. The HR Settings walk and the control register review (Chapters 2-3).
24. The retirement-dates read from the Retirement Age computation (Chapter 2).
25. The attrition and exit-theme annual review to the owner (module 7).

The calendar's rule. The payroll track's month-eleven lesson applies to the whole HR year: the annual block is scheduled in writing before its season, owners named per line, the December items placed clear of the payroll year-end's own pressure. A calendar line without an owner is a hope; the register (Chapter 3) gives every line one.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The HR reports and data protection
lessons.html:
Two closing disciplines: what the function reports, and how it protects what it holds.

1. The standing reports, as management data. Each derives from records the modules maintain; each goes to its reader on the calendar's cadence; all follow the data-not-editorial rule.

1. Headcount — the Employee list grouped by company, branch, department, designation, type, Status = Active (module 1's lookup); trended quarterly.
2. Joiners and leavers — the monthly lists (module 1), annualised into the attrition read: leavers by reason, unit, tenure band (module 7).
3. Absence and lateness patterns — module 3's monthly summaries, trended.
4. Leave position — balances by unit ahead of peak seasons; the year's carry, lapse, encashment, and usage per type (module 4's data pack).
5. Recruitment effectiveness — time-to-hire, source effectiveness, offer-acceptance rates (module 2's registers).
6. Performance distributions — per cycle, calibrated (module 5).
7. Training delivery and compliance currency — the plan read and the expiry buckets (module 6).
8. The lifecycle page — events, scheduled-event health, grievance ages (module 7).

The construction rule: every figure on every report is a count or computation over records, reproducible by the reader from the named source. A report figure that cannot be traced to records in two lookups fails the programme's standard.

2. Data protection across the HR doctypes. HR holds the system's most personal data. The rules, gathered:

1. The access matrix per doctype: Employee (HR write; scoped read per function; self-service for own record), the appraisal and feedback doctypes (the disclosure rule — module 5), grievances (handling roles only — module 7), applicant records (recruiting roles — module 2), health and identification fields (the narrowest read that the work requires — module 1). The matrix is written, configured, and included in the sysadmin track's quarterly access recertification.
2. The retention conventions, decided and executed: employment records per the statutory periods (the payroll track's seven-year discipline governs the overlapping records); rejected-applicant data per the recruitment convention (module 2); grievance records per the policy. Each convention written, each executed on the calendar.
3. The handling rules: documents on records, not personal drives; the one-recipient rule for anything personal (the payroll track's delivery discipline applied in kind); changes to personal data on the employee's written instruction (module 1's governed fields); and the standing principle — data collected for a purpose is used for that purpose, and a new use (the mobile checkin's location capture — Chapter 2) is stated in policy before it is switched on.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Multi-company HR
lessons.html:
Where the site carries more than one company, HR respects the legal separation — the payroll track's module 8 rule, executed on the HR records.

1. The per-company records.

1. Employment is per company (module 1, Chapter 3): the Employee record belongs to its employing entity; the dual-role person is two records or a documented cross-charge per the accountant's design.
2. The organisational masters split where they must: Departments are per company by design (module 1, Chapter 2); Designations and Employment Types are shared masters used across companies; Holiday Lists are built per company where the working calendars differ.
3. The policy machinery is per company: Leave Periods and Leave Policies attach per company (module 4); a group-wide policy is entered as matching per-company records, and a deliberate difference between companies is a written policy difference, not a configuration accident found later.
4. The pipelines and cycles scope per company: Staffing Plans, Job Openings, Appraisal Cycles, and Training Events carry their company; the reads filter accordingly.

2. The cross-company reads. The owner of a group reads both views:

1. Per company — every report in Chapter 5 filtered to the entity, which is also the only view an entity's auditor sees.
2. Group totals — headcount, attrition, and cost views summed across entities for the owner's page, always constructed from the per-company figures (the group number that cannot be decomposed back to its entities fails the traceability standard).

3. The movement between companies. The inter-company transfer (module 7, Chapter 2) is the boundary's crossing point, run as the exit-and-join it legally is: the origin company's closure lines (payroll settlement per its rules, the statutory tail in its name), the destination's joiner lines (the verification, the assignment, the policy allocations, the compliance obligations), and the lifecycle document coordinating the organisational side. The person's history remains readable across both records — the movement record notes the crossing with both references.

4. The shared-services note. Where one HR operator serves all entities (the common small-group arrangement), the operator's access spans companies while every record they touch stays entity-pure — the operator is shared; the data is not. The access matrix states the span; the recertification confirms it; and the per-entity audit answer (Chapter 5's rule) is unaffected by who operates, which is the purpose of the whole design.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The handover test
lessons.html:
The programme's standing final test, applied to HR: could a competent successor, given only the function's documentation, run next month's HR correctly?

1. The artifact list the test reads. Gathered from the modules:

1. The Employee register with its verification comments and the hygiene filter procedure (module 1).
2. The recruitment pipeline records and the offer/onboarding templates (module 2).
3. The Holiday Lists, Shift Types with their configuration notes, the per-location marking procedures with named markers and deputies (module 3).
4. The leave type register, the policies, the annual round procedure, the close-date rules (module 4).
5. The appraisal templates with decision references, the cycle calendar and procedures (module 5).
6. The programme and compliance registers, the training plan, the result-entry rule (module 6).
7. The separation and onboarding templates, the lifecycle procedures, the movement record (module 7).
8. The settings record, the control register, the HR calendar, the access matrix and retention conventions (this module).

2. The absence test. Run deliberately and soon — a planned week with the operator reachable, per the payroll track's rule:

1. The trained backstop (the cross-trained deputy or the payroll operator's HR-literate colleague, per the business's arrangement) runs one full cycle from the documentation: the daily and weekly reads, a joiner's verification if one lands, the records-close block with the payroll handover, whatever the calendar serves that week.
2. The operator answers no question the file should answer; every question asked is a documentation finding, fixed on return.
3. The test's pass is the month closing on the calendar with the evidence in its locations — confirmed by the register's owner sample the following week.

3. The annual confirmation. The control register's review (Chapter 3) confirms yearly: the backstop's training current, the artifact list complete against this chapter's list, the calendar's owners all present in the business (the owner row naming a leaver is itself a finding the movement record should have caught).

4. Why this closes the track. The HR function holds the records every other function starts from — the payroll run selects from module 1's register; the sysadmin's access follows module 7's events; the accounts' cost lines follow module 1's cost centers. An HR function that lives in one person's memory makes every one of those functions hostage to the same absence. The track built the alternative module by module: masters verified at entry, events as documents, reads on a calendar, evidence in named locations — and the handover test is the proof that the construction holds without its builder, which is the professional standard this certification names.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: the HealthTrade HR year close
lessons.html:
This chapter applies Chapters 2-7 to HealthTrade's year. Configuration values and outcomes are listed per step.

Step 1 — the settings walk (Chapter 2). Run with the MD in one sitting; nine fields recorded with owner, date, reason. Key decisions: Employee Naming By confirmed as naming series (set at implementation, untouched); Retirement Age entered from the employment policy — the computation immediately lists one approaching date four years out, which joins the annual read; backdated leave restricted with the permitted role held by HR (the sickness-on-return lane documented); Check Vacancies switched on (the plan validation had been advisory — now enforced); mobile checkin left off with the reason recorded (no field staff yet; to be revisited with the policy when vans get route staff).

Step 2 — the register and calendar (Chapters 3-4). The control register assembles in an afternoon: twenty-three rows across the seven modules, each with owner, cadence, evidence location. The calendar publishes with the register: the annual block scheduled in writing in October — the Holiday List build and the leave entitlement round placed in November and early December, deliberately clear of the payroll year-end. The MD's first unannounced sample: two rows (the blank-field filters, the compliance read) — both evidenced in one lookup each.

Step 3 — the annual block executes (Chapter 4). November: the 2027 Holiday Lists built, the assignment sweep confirms every Active employee on a current list. Early December: the 2027 Leave Period, the policy confirmed unchanged, Policy Assignments run — ninety-three allocations (thirty-one staff by then × three rows), completeness verified; carry-forward processes with the cap, and the year-turn communication states the lapse rule. The training plan for 2027 drafts from the three intakes — the compliance lines placed from known expiries, four appraisal needs carried from the cycle, one initiative line — and the MD approves it with its cost column.

Step 4 — the reports settle into rhythm (Chapter 5). The quarterly owner pack standardises at six pages: headcount trend, attrition (three leavers for the year: two resignations, one contract end — by reason, unit, tenure), the leave data pack, compliance currency (100% current at year-end, the retake closed in Q3), the training plan read (eleven of twelve lines delivered and resulted; one slipped with cause), the lifecycle page (zero scheduled-event lapses for the year). Every figure traces in two lookups; the MD's stated test — ask any number, see its records — passes on each pack.

Step 5 — data protection (Chapter 5). The access matrix written and configured across the HR doctypes; grievance access confirmed to the handling roles; the retention conventions decided (rejected applicants: eighteen months; the clearing run for the first time removes forty-one records past convention). The matrix joins the sysadmin's Q1 recertification.

Step 6 — the absence test (Chapter 7). A planned week in February: the accounts assistant (cross-trained through the quarter) runs the calendar's week from the file — the daily reads, the weekly sheet read, the records-close block into payroll. Three questions get asked; three documentation fixes result (the sheet read's filter steps written down; the LWP handover's format specified; one evidence location corrected on the register). The month closes on the calendar; the owner sample the following week confirms the evidence. The MD's year note records the structural result: the HR function ran a week without its operator, answered every pack question from records, and enters the new year with its calendar, register, and backstop in place.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common errors and the track's eight rules
lessons.html:
The structural layer's recurring failures, then the track assembled.

Error 1 — the unexamined settings. Symptom: approval flags, backdating permissions, and validation switches in whatever state implementation left them; behaviours nobody chose governing everybody's records. Correction: the walk run, each field decided and recorded. Prevention: the annual re-walk with the register review.

Error 2 — controls as habits. Symptom: reads that happen when remembered; evidence that needs assembly; oversight that must ask. Correction: the control register built — owner, cadence, evidence location per row. Prevention: the owner's unannounced samples and the annual review.

Error 3 — the calendar in one head. Symptom: the entitlement round remembered in January; holiday lists built after the year turned; annual items colliding with the payroll year-end. Correction: the calendar written with owners, the annual block scheduled before its season. Prevention: the October scheduling rule and the register's owner column.

Error 4 — reports as impressions. Symptom: management pages built from recollection and adjustment; figures that cannot be traced; the same question answered differently twice. Correction: every figure rebuilt as a count over named records. Prevention: the two-lookup traceability standard applied to every pack.

Error 5 — data handled by convenience. Symptom: personal documents in inboxes and drives; access accumulated, never recertified; retention indefinite by default; capabilities switched on without policy. Correction: the matrix written and configured, the conventions decided and executed, the handling rules applied. Prevention: the matrix in the quarterly recertification and the conventions on the calendar.

Error 6 — the indispensable operator. Symptom: HR stops when one person is away; the joiner unverified, the close missed, the reads skipped for a week and the gaps discovered downstream. Correction: the artifact list completed, the backstop trained. Prevention: the deliberate absence test, run soon, its questions fixed as documentation findings.

The track's eight rules.

1. The Employee record is the master every HR and payroll document reads — built from the organisational masters, completed from source documents, verified before first use, retired by status, and kept complete by the standing filters.
2. Hiring runs through the pipeline — vacancies approved on the plan, candidates processed on recorded statuses, assessments structured and same-day, offers issued from the document with complete terms, and joiners onboarded on a generated checklist confirmed before the joining date.
3. Attendance is recorded per day per employee — checkins as evidence, the Shift Type's settings as the ruling, manual locations marked daily by named people, corrections through the request lane, and the month complete at the records close.
4. Leave is entitlement executed as records — types configured from the written policy, allocations generated by the annual policy round, applications decided in the system by the records close, pay-affecting leave documented like the pay decision it is, and every balance answerable from the ledger.
5. Performance is assessed on records — templates weighted by decision, cycles run on a published calendar, scores computed from confirmed goals and submitted feedback, calibrated through the raters, and handed to the decision lanes as information, never as execution.
6. Training is delivered as records — programmes catalogued once, events run from the plan with full tables, results entered within the week, compliance tracked by arithmetic on passing results, and every question answered from the rows as kept.
7. Lifecycle events are documents — transfers and promotions applying their property rows from honest dates, grievances entered as stated and resolved on the record, separations run as generated checklists beside the payroll exit, and every scheduled event decided on time from the standing reads.
8. The HR function survives its operator — settings written, controls registered, the year on its calendar, data protected by matrix and convention, every report traceable in two lookups, and the whole function proven by absence.

This completes the HR Professional track.
